column121: During a CFII training flight in my aircraft; I was teaching my student how to give vectors to final for the RNAV XX approach into ZZZ with WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System) disabled. We; Aircraft X; a Piper PA-28 gave ourselves VTF (Vectors to Final) at 2000ft MSL approximately 8nm NE from the airport. We turned into and captured the FAC (Flight Augmentation Computer) of RNAV XX with no other traffic on an approach into ZZZ for runway XX. We descended 500fpm until reaching 1500ft MSL; the FAF altitude listed on the approach plate. We were driving to the final approach fix; level at 1500msl approx 6nm from the airport when Aircraft Y made a 10nm final call over the ZZZ CTAF frequency. The Citation did not appear on our traffic map on the G1000 nxi MFD (Multi-funcion Flight Display)  until he was nearly 1000ft above us and I saw the traffic on the MFD display a downward arrow; indicating the Citation's descent. In a matter of less than 30 seconds; the Citation was approximately less than 1 mile behind Aircraft X; and 500ft above me. This is when I got the TCAS alert and immediately grabbed flight controls and took evasive action; banking the aircraft nearly 60 degrees and turning 90 degrees to avoid a collision from the Citation.My airspeed at the time of the evasion was 78kts and the citation; Aircraft Y was 201kts according to ADS-B exchange data. I started the evasion at XA:36:30. If I had not taken the aggressive and immediately maneuver; I confidently believe the Citation would have crashed into me; Aircraft X and killing myself and my student. No radio contact was established with the pilot of Aircraft Y  outside of his initial 10nm final call over CTAF and a short final radio call that I could pick up. After rolling wings level I made a radio call telling the pilot of Aircraft Y that I had to break off the approach to avoid being hit by him. He never replied to the radio call. I gave VTF again for the approach into ZZZ and landed safely. Prevailing conditions of the flight were VFR; cloud ceilings were approximately 3000-4000AGL. My aircraft; Aircraft X maintained VFR cloud clearance requirements of 500ft below cloud layers at all times during this flight. I do not believe the pilot of Aircraft Y ever saw us on the approach. IF the pilot of Aircraft Y was on an IFR flight plan shooting an approach into an airport with a known flight school; with pilots making radio calls at every phase of flight; I question why he would shoot an IAP going that fast; or why ATC would clear him for the approach while my aircraft is on the final approach segment.
column123: Aircraft: Cessna Citation CJ3+ (Aircraft X)Operation: Part 91 IFRDeparture: ZZZ1Destination: ZZZI departed ZZZ1 as PIC of a Cessna Citation CJ3+; Aircraft X; operating under an IFR flight plan to ZZZ. The clearance was direct ZZZZZ; then direct ZZZ; maintaining 3;000 feet. We picked up our IFR clearance at approximately 1;500 feet after departure.Weather conditions were IMC above approximately 2;500-3;000 feet MSL. While level at 3;000 feet in IMC enroute to ZZZZZ; we were handed off from ZZZ Center to ZZZ Approach Control. ZZZ Approach instructed us to climb to 3;400 feet and cleared us direct ZZZZZ for the RNAV (GPS) Runway XX approach into ZZZ; with a crossing restriction of at or above 3;300 feet at ZZZZZ. We complied with all instructions.Multiple aircraft were observed operating in the traffic pattern at ZZZ via ADS-B; and we had been monitoring this traffic since departure. One aircraft in particular appeared aligned with Runway XX and possibly flying the same RNAV approach. Upon reaching ZZZZZ and beginning descent; we broke out of IMC at approximately 2;800-3;000 feet MSL.At approximately 10 miles from the airport; we reported a 10-mile final for the RNAV Runway XX approach. ZZZ Approach issued a traffic advisory for an aircraft approximately four to five miles ahead of us and below; descending. We had already observed this aircraft on ADS-B and acquired it visually after breaking out of the clouds.Based on closure rate; we determined we were overtaking the traffic ahead and that continuing straight-in would likely reduce spacing. ZZZ Approach was not in communication with that aircraft; and it appeared to be operating VFR.To improve spacing and integrate safely with pattern traffic; we elected to cancel IFR and continue visually. Approximately 5-6 miles from the airport; we initiated a left turn to maneuver toward the published ZZZZZ1 visual reporting point; which is identified in the enhanced operating procedures as the preferred VFR entry for a 45-degree downwind to Runway XX.As we began the left turn; the aircraft ahead also initiated a left turn. At that time; we were approximately three miles behind and slightly above that aircraft. No prior radio transmission was heard from that aircraft indicating its intentions. The turn resulted in a temporary converging flight path.Upon assessing the geometry and maintaining visual contact; I determined the safest course of action was to discontinue the left turn and re-establish on the extended final approach course. We remained in visual contact at all times.During the convergence; a momentary TCAS Resolution Advisory was generated. The advisory was brief and consistent with the converging geometry. Visual separation was maintained; and the RA cleared as lateral spacing increased. No maneuver beyond normal course correction was required.The other aircraft continued turning away from our course and was no longer a factor. Shortly thereafter; the aircraft transmitted that it was breaking off the approach. Another aircraft on downwind stated that he would extend his downwind to provide spacing. We reported a 4-mile final and landed uneventfully at ZZZ. Visual separation was maintained at all times; and the flight concluded without further incident.Contributing Factors:IMC-to-VMC transition during approach phaseHigh volume of VFR training traffic at a non-towered airportMixed IFR arrivals and VFR practice approach operationsClosure rate differences between turbine IFR traffic and training aircraftLimited radio coordination from some aircraft in the patternHuman Factors: Situational awareness was maintained through continuous ADS-B monitoring and visual acquisition upon breakout. The combination of IMC-to-VMC transition; closure rate on slower traffic; and multiple aircraft in the pattern created compressed decision-making during a high-workload phase of flight. The brief TCAS RA reinforced the importance of conservative spacing when integratingmixed IFR and VFR traffic.Safety Consideration: This event highlights the operational challenges of mixing IFR arrivals with high volumes of VFR training traffic in marginal VFR conditions at non-towered airports. While conditions were legally VFR; arriving aircraft descending from higher altitudes and higher speeds may require instrument procedures for descent; which can compress spacing when pattern traffic is established ahead.Increased emphasis on communication clarity and conservative spacing during such mixed-traffic scenarios may help reduce similar occurrences.Corrective Actions / Lessons Learned: Consider earlier speed reduction or spacing adjustments when overtaking slower traffic on instrument approaches into busy training environments.Continue proactive ADS-B monitoring and early visual acquisition during IMC-to-VMC transitions.Maintain conservative lateral and longitudinal spacing when traffic intentions are unclear.Exercise heightened vigilance when integrating IFR arrival profiles into active VFR pattern operations.

I was preoccupied with my other arrivals and I didn't understand why they couldn't keep Aircraft X  in the pattern when they had 1 aircraft; so I verified that they 'could not keep the aircraft in the pattern;' to which they replied that they could not. While focusing on the other IFR aircraft and making sure they were avoiding the random VFR targets out there; I noticed a VFR target seemingly appearing to depart ZZZ's class D.  However; this target was several hundred feet below Aircraft X and I had no indication that the VFR target would continue their climb; and at this moment; Aircraft X appeared to be in the safest position compared to my other IFR targets.  I shipped Aircraft X to the tower so they could work them in.  Recommendation: We need controlled / protected airspace north of ZZZ.  This area is a mid-air waiting to happen.  We've been told that we can't lower the Bravo airspace out there.  Nor can we create a SATR or otherwise.  We just seem to be in this unsafe situation in perpetuity.  We all see the solution; but the FAA is silent and does not seem to care about fixing the problem.  Every controller can tell you the solution; but only the FAA can act on it; and unfortunately; they sit idle until two airplanes collide.  I'm not talking local FAA.  I'm talking big FAA... the only ones who can make the airspace safer.Get some protected airspace out there in that area ASAP - two airplanes will collide at some point without it.

The issue I have is imbedded later on within the same NOTAM text it indirectly addresses a totally different approach; the ILS 36C. It says the I-DQG ILS or glideslope out of service. There are at least 2 or 3 other NOTAMs for Runway 36C but none of them call out the glideslope except for the RNAV NOTAM. You do not use the I-DQS ILS for the RNAV approach.Last night we were given a late runway change to the visual to 36C after setting up for and briefing the approach to 36L. column121: - This was a two Captain flight crew operating flight #XXXX; with service from ZZZ to ZZZ1. This was the second flight of the day in the airplane and no major mechanical abnormalities were experienced during the first flight. The only notable event was a TLO light (Left Side) that illuminated during cruise. Person A  served as the First Officer and Pilot Monitoring during both the first and second flights. I had not flown in 18 days as a result of a previous reported incident and Person A  was helping me regain proficiency in the airplane.- In ZZZ; the aircraft started up normally and we taxied to the runup area on the 1 taxiway. Upon completing the Before Takeoff Checklist; and with both engines within all parameters; we were given taxi instructions to RWY XX and then cleared for departure. - Both engines eventually developed full power at 103 percent and we rotated around 72 knots. I noted that the engines were surging at times but appeared to smooth out with more airspeed and prior to rotation. When we were around 200 feet above the runway; the left engine began to make a loud popping noise and the power reduced to around 70%.- There was a substantial amount of runway left in front of us as RWY XX is 10;400 feet long. Since we had a headwind and variable crosswind gusting to 22 knots; I initially pulled back power in order to land back on the runway. This is what I had briefed in the Takeoff Briefing.- At this point; Person A stated that we should keep flying and to continue our climb straight ahead. I considered it and then moved both throttles back to full power. We started climbing again. The engine popped one more time but did not lose power. - We were able to climb without incident to 1;000 ft and Person A  notified ATC that we needed to return to the airport for landing. ATC was able to accommodate us immediately back for a left pattern for a return landing on RWY XX. The landing and rollout were uneventful and we notified ZZZ Ops that we had returned. We also informed them that Aircraft X needed maintenance attention and was not airworthy. We also told them that we would need another aircraft to fly our passengers to ZZZ1.- Person A contacted Maintenance Control while I wrote up the incident in the Aircraft Maintenance Log. Person A  then contacted Operations  to inform them of the situation. He was then instructed to contact Person B; the On-Call Duty Manager. He did so and we both chatted with Person B on speaker phone. He supported our decision to return and guided us through the process.- We obtained another aircraft and were able to fly our passengers to ZZZ1 without incident. We remained in our same crew positions for the second attempt of this flight; with myself as Pilot Flying and Person A  as Pilot Monitoring.

column121: While at the gate in ZZZ the aircraft displayed a L OIL LVL LOW status message; with the left engine at shut off prior to blocking out. We (the first officer and I) checked the oil level on the menu page. It indicated that the left engine oil level was at 51%. After referencing the CRJ 900 QRH 0-XX Table 0-1: Oil Level Indication and Duration Table; we determined to be in the 10 hour flight range and above the Do not dispatch" minimum. We continued with the flight as normal. The APU was deferred on this flight so we executed a right engine start at the gate using ground supply air and electrical power. After the right engine start was complete; we pushed back from the gate and taxied to the XXR deice pad on a single engine using all standard procedures. Completed Type 1 deicing process and then began our taxi to runway XXL for departure via Taxiway 1. While on Taxiway 1; the First Officer and I completed a cross bleed start to the left engine using bleed air from the right engine as directed by the QRH. Once the left engine start was complete; all normal delayed start and before takeoff checklist and procedures were completed. In addition to that; the oil level of both engines were check via the menu page and found to be at an acceptable level for departure. Departed runway XXL at ZZZ with no adverse indications. Completed a normal climb to our cruise altitude of FL310 with no adverse indications. Following standard procedures and checklist at every phase of flight. Sometime after reaching our cruise altitude; about 10 minutes after level at FL310; I (the captain and pilot flying) checked the oil levels once again via the menu page. Upon checking the oil levels I found that the left engine was at 15%. We began monitoring the left engine indications as directed by the CRJ900 QRH 0-XX Table 0-1. At that time I began turning to the L ENG OIL PRESS checklist in the QRH just in case it would be needed. About 2-3 minutes after the First Officer and I began monitoring the left engine indications; we received a L ENG OIL PRESS warning message; chime and aural alert. At that time I handed the QRH to the First Officer; I remained the pilot and took over radio communication control; and we began running the CRJ 900 QRH 1-XY L ENG OIL PRESS and subsequent CRJ 900 QRH 1-XZ ENGINE FAILURE/INFLIGHT ENGINE SHUTDOWN checklist. Because both pilots confirmed that the L ENG OIL PRESS warning message was present and the oil pressure was below limits we continued with the intentional shutdown as directed by the checklist. All the while we remained in constant contact with ATC. Primarily ZZZCenter. After the left engine was brought to ideal the aircraft was unable to maintain FL310. So; with clearance from ATC; we descended to FL250. By the time we reached FL250 the left engine was fully shutdown. The aircraft was able to maintain FL250 with right thrust set to tracking. But I elected to descend lower to FL210 in an effort to "take it easy" on the operative engine. Once at FL210 all checklist were completed and that is when I requested priority handling with ZZZ center; informed dispatch and maintenance control via ACARS; and notified the flight attendants of the situation. We did try to contact dispatch through ARINC (Radio) frequency XXX.XX; but had no reply from City X radio. When informing the flight attendants; I told them "the left engine was intentionally shutdown by us to prevent damage. The aircraft is still flying perfectly normal. We are counting to ZZZ1 as planned. We are going to land at ZZZ1 and taxi to the gate just like a normal flight. At this time; the is no need to inform the passengers. If there is need I will inform them. You don't not need to prepare for an evacuation. If anything changes to the situation I will update you". After the flight attendants were informed; the First Officer and I reconfirmed the decision to continue to ZZZ1. We completed all briefings and checklists as we made our descent into ZZZ1. While talking toZZZ approach control; we requested to land on runway XY due to favorable headwinds. Upon switching to tower control; they informed us that fire and rescue would be standing by on the ground. The aircraft was landed safely on runway XZ and made a right turnoff at 2. After landing fire and rescue asked if we needed assistance. I informed them that no assistance was required and they replied by saying they would follow us to the ramp and then head back to the station. We taxied to gate XX; parked; shutdown the right engine and passed the aircraft over to station maintenance personnel.Cause:  The conditions that led to a loss of oil pressure inflight are unknown to me at this time. The post flight inspection revealed a large oil stain under the cowling of the left engine. Indicating a possible oil leak that possibly led to the loss of oil pressure."

column121: During engine start; we received ENG1 GEN FAULT. We followed ECAM procedures and it came back online. I entered it in the ELB (Electronic Logbook); called Dispatch; and finished the procedure with Maintenance Control. We called for taxi; was cleared to Runway XX; taxied out; and departed. At approximately 1500' both the FO (First Officer) and I noticed a sort of shimmy; as though the gear was still down; flaps were down; or maybe the speed brakes were out; but all was normal. It did not seem to me like an engine vibration and we didn't notice any parameters showing high vibes; so we continued. On climb out; beginning at ~3000'; received multiple transient ENG 1 THRUST LEVER DISAGREE ECAMs. All engine parameters were normal on both engines and the thrust levers were perfectly aligned; so I felt that continuing was the best plan. On the 4th or 5th ECAM; it stayed up almost long enough to run the full procedure; but then it went away again. It came back again as we were passing ~23;000'. It was no longer transient and I decided we needed to start back to the field. I asked the FO to pass the info to Dispatch. They messaged back that they would get the ball rolling. ATC turned us back and began our descent. The ECAM cleared; but we had already started turning back so we continued. We requested priority handling in the turn back to ZZZ. To this point; both engines had been performing normally and it seemed like it may have been an indication issue. On level off; ENG 1 did not spool up; staying at flight idle. The plane commanded LEVER MCT (Maximum Continuous Thrust); and performance went into EO (Engine-Out). At this point; I asked the FO to request ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) support upon arrival. They said the trucks would be ready. We revisited procedures and both agreed that everything had been completed; to include a report to the (LFA) Lead Flight Attendant. We were vectored to the ILS XX; but the tailwind during the return pushed us too much and we were vectored around for further descent. Upon the next vectors; I thought ATC had requested a ten degree turn to the left; which I did and then our course was promptly blown too close to the localizer - apparently they had given me a RIGHT course correction. They vectored us out once again and gave us much more room to catch the localizer. We commenced the approach; and landed without any further issues. At some point; when were exiting the runway I smelled something odd; so I requested ARFF scan ENG 1 just in case there was something internal to the nacelle. ARFF completed the entire aircraft scan and reported no further issues with the FLIR. I requested to continue into the terminal; to which we were given clearance. At this point; a passenger got up and used the bathroom before the FAs could stop them. Once they sat back down; we continued to taxi to the gate; shut down normally; and deplaned the pax. I'm fairly certain; with everything going on and the previously transient ECAM; something was missed in the approach. We revisited the procedures; although we briefed the passengers later than I would have liked; making sure all the information was covered. I feel like everything was covered; maybe poorly and out of sequence; but so many things were happening that I was doing a lot just staying in front of the problem and making sure that I was prioritizing flying the aircraft. We were constantly checking in with each other to make sure each of us were up to speed and also SA.
column123: After ENG 1 started and stabilized; we received an ECAM: ENG 1 GEN FAULT. We completed the ECAM procedures; and the generator came back online. We contacted Dispatch; completed the ELB (Electronic Logbook) entry; and cross-verified the information with each other. We were cleared to taxi to Runway XX and subsequently departed.During climb; at approximately 1;000-1;500 feet AGL; we noticed a brief irregular vibration; similar to what it would feel like if a gear door were open or the speed brakes were partially extended. All system parameters appeared normal; and the vibration lasted less than 10 seconds. We elected to continue the climb.Beginning at approximately 3;000 feet; we received an ECAM: ENG 1 THRUST LEVER DISAGREE. The message cleared few seconds later. We verified engine parameters; thrust lever positions; and associated indications; all were normal. We assessed it as a transient condition and continued the climb. The same ECAM message reappeared multiple times (approximately 4-5 times). Then the ECAM remained long enough to begin and finish the ECAM procedure; but it cleared again.At approximately FL230; the ECAM returned. We requested ATC to level off to properly accomplish the checklist and assess the situation. While leveling at approximately FL280; we decided to return to ZZZ. We immediately notified Dispatch via ACARS of the ECAM message and our decision to return to ZZZ. We requested priority handling with ATC and advised them of our intention to return; including souls on board and fuel remaining. ATC cleared us direct to ZZZ.Until and during descent; both engines initially displayed matched parameters within normal limits. However; while descending; ENG 1 remained at idle and did not respond as expected. The system prompted us to set the thrust lever to MCT (Maximum Continuous Thrust). Considering the ENG 1 condition and the overweight landing; we requested ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) support from ATC.We completed all required coordination with ATC; Dispatch; the flight attendants; and passengers. After setting up for the approach and completing the approach briefing; we requested vectors to allow time to accomplish the overweight landing checklist. Upon completion; we cross-verified all checklist items to ensure nothing was missed.We were vectored for the ILS Runway XX but were unable to intercept the localizer. Requested another vector; cleared for the approach.We landed on Runway XX and vacated the runway. We stopped on Taxiway 1 to allow fire trucks to inspect the aircraft. ARFF reported no abnormalities. We contacted Operations frequency to advise them of our situation and assigned gate. We then taxied to the gate; shut down the engines; and the passengers deplaned without further incident. Being only approximately 50-60 miles from the departure airport; the repeated ECAM messages and evolving situation created a high workload environment. It was not a comfortable experience operationally. In hindsight; I could have taken additional time to review the Manual more thoroughly and attempt to gain a deeper; more systematic understanding of the malfunction. We also could have delegated tasks more efficiently to better manage workload and reduce task saturation.This report serves as a reflection on the event and improvement. While we strive for precision and professionalism; we recognize that we are not immune to human limitations.

Shortly after reducing power and deacceleration the CA looked up and acknowledged the airplane crossing the runway and took controls while verbalizing reject reject; my controls. We had stopped on taxiway 1 initially clear of runway XXR while CA made PA to passengers to remain seated and aware of situation. The controller shortly asked after if we would like to return to gate or taxi back for take off and we contacted back that we needed to run checklist and cool off brakes. column121: I am submitting this report to document an event that occurred during a ferry flight from ZZZ.I was assigned to Reserve Availability Period 1 and was called in for Standby Position 1. I received a call from Customer Service indicating that there was a ferry flight from Gate XX that needed to proceed. Upon arriving at the gate; I met Captain A; who informed me that he was still awaiting a flight release and that there was no gate agent available. I sought assistance from the neighboring gate to gain access to the aircraft; and we both began our duties to prepare for the flight. After completing my walk-around; I performed the cabin equipment check. With our duties completed; we both proceeded to close the main cabin door using the checklist; and we confirmed the door status as green on the EICAS status page.We did not realize that the vent flaps on the remaining three cabin doors were not closed and secured. Being new to ferry operations; I initially interpreted the EICAS messages for the remaining doors as indicating that the slides were not armed; which I mistook for the vent flap issue. We continued to set up for our flight; and on departure we received clearance to climb and maintain FL210.During the climb through 10;500 feet; we encountered a Cabin HIGH ALT warning. Captain A immediately advised ATC that we would level off at 10;000 feet to address the issue. I; as the FO and pilot flying; disconnected the autopilot in an attempt to halt the climb and descend to 10;000 feet. I did not reset the altitude selector to 10;000 feet; and the aircraft briefly accelerated to 325 knots while descending from 11;500 feet to 10;000 feet. Captain A then held the throttles at idle to assist with deceleration and directed me to set 10;000 feet in the altitude selector. The aircraft returned to a normal speed; and the over-speed condition lasted approximately 3-5 seconds.ATC asked about our intentions three times; we confirmed that we would remain at 10;000 feet while we assessed and addressed the issue. After the third inquiry; ATC vectored us to our assigned heading. Following stabilization; I conducted a positive exchange of controls so that I could proceed to close the vent flaps on the remaining doors. Cabin altitude subsequently returned to normal; and we continued the flight without further incident.Cause: I am providing a cause narrative for the ferry flight from ZZZ to document the factors that contributed to the cabin pressurization event and to outline corrective actions. The sequence of events revealed a chain of contributing factors centered on ferry-flight procedures; crew experience; and situational awareness during the abnormal situation.The root cause began with an incomplete preflight and door-status verification for ferry operations. Vent flaps on the three non-primary cabin doors were not closed and secured; a condition that went unidentified prior to departure. This oversight stemmed from a lack of ferry-specific checks and limited experience; which led to the misinterpretation of EICAS messages as indicating slide arming rather than the actual vent flap status. I initially assumed that EICAS messages related to the other cabin doors pertained to slide arming; causing the vent flap issue to be overlooked until the event unfolded.During the climb; I disconnected the autopilot and did not reset the altitude selector to 10;000 feet; allowing a brief overspeed condition as we descended from 11;500 feet toward 10;000 feet. This indicated a delay in crew coordination and procedures during a high-workload; time-critical event. The situation was further stressed by limited ferry-flight experience and delayed identification of the vent flap closure issue and misreading of cues from the EICAS system. In addition; the preflight process did not include a definitive check of vent flap status on all cabin doors; increasing the likelihood of an undetected vent-flap exposure. Communication with ATC under stress also highlighted the need for clear; decisive actions; as initial exchanges were hampered by moments of uncertainty before we could present a unified plan.Immediate corrective actions were taken once the situation was stabilized. A positive exchange of controls allowed me to close the vent flaps on the remaining doors; after which cabin pressure returned to normal and the flight proceeded without further incident. The aircraft was stabilized at 10;000 feet; and ATC vectored us to a safe heading; ensuring continued safe operations.Suggestions: During the recent operation; we faced pressure to expedite departure; but we determined that slowing the pace was necessary to maintain safety and accuracy. We also recognize that we could have leveraged available resources more effectively; including maintenance; dispatch; and company operations; to aid decision-making and risk assessment.Going forward; I have learned that when any aspect of a procedure or condition is in question; it is essential to slow down and seek clarification before proceeding. This approach will help ensure we address potential issues thoroughly and maintain safe; compliant operations.

column121: On approach into BFI; we were cleared for the visual approach to runway 32L. At about 1;000' AGL; the BFI tower controller issued us a traffic advisory for Aircraft Y in right closed traffic for runway 32R; the close parallel runway; and reported that we 'might see him when he turns base.' I recall seeing Aircraft Y turning right crosswind but I can't recall if the Captain reported 'traffic in sight' to ATC or not. When we were at about 400' AGL; I saw Aircraft Y turn right base directly at us; about 200' above us; and probably 0.25 NM to our east (right side). Aircraft Y continued to descend; momentarily leveled off on base; and then turned final for runway 32R. I estimate that Aircraft Y got within 100' vertically and 400' horizontally of us. I had visual contact with Aircraft Y the entire time but when Aircraft Y turned right onto final; the Aircraft Y pilot could not see us due to the aircraft's low-wing design. It was very concerning that the Aircraft Y pilot decided to turn base directly at us instead of extending downwind until passing us. Trying to hand-fly the aircraft on the visual approach and continually watch Aircraft Y as it flew directly at us was very distracting and was not safe.Suggestions: The parallel runways at BFI are spaced only 375' apart; centerline to centerline. With that in mind; the BFI tower controller should have instructed Aircraft Y to extend downwind in an effort to stagger arrivals to the closely-spaced parallel runways. It should be standard operating procedure for BFI ATC to ensure that arrivals are staggered and separation is maintained. 'Maintain visual separation' continues to provide subjective distances of adequate separation for pilots to maintain. The Aircraft Y pilot should have maintained adequate visual separation with us and extended their downwind or slowed down in order to do so because we were on a straight-in approach. More education for GA pilots on flying traffic patterns at airports with closely-spaced parallel runways could help.

column121: We started our day two of the trip with two legs on Day 0 in ZZZ. This day we were scheduled to operate ZZZ-ZZZ1 then from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. Initially the inbound aircraft to ZZZ was delayed. Shortly after We claimed the aircraft and started the trip We found the APU to be INOP and MEL-ed (49-XX-XXX). This was observed both in the Engineering change request form as well as informed by the incoming crew. Aside from that MEL the aircraft didn't have any issues or malfunctions. On the ground at ZZZ we observed ' L OIL LEVEL LO' status message. After confirming the indication we checked with QRH and confirmed that the aircraft was still good to go and within the limitations specified in the table in QRH . The flight from ZZZ into ZZZ1 was operated as normal and without any issues. After getting to ZZZ1 and preparing for the second and last flight of the day; a preflight inspection was conducted by me (FO) and nothing out of the ordinary was found. No leakages of either engines or any other fluids were observed. After boarding and getting ready for pushback; We once again checked the Left Oil Level and it showed 51% (engine off); once again we checked the table  and found that the duration of available oil until next service is 10 hours for that quantity. We made a mental note and discussed to let Maintenance know once we got to ZZZ2. Shortly before pushback; We observed snow flurries starting to fall and decided to get de-iced prior to departure. We taxied single engine onto the de-ice pad (XXR); after getting done with de-icing we started our taxi for runway XYL in ZZZ1 and did a cross-bleed start on the left engine. Before; during and after the engine start all indications were showing within the normal parameters. After going through our procedures and checklists We then continued onto the runway and prepared for Take off. During the take off and climb Phases all indications were showing operations within normal parameters. shortly after reaching our cruising altitude of FL310 ( approximately 10-12 minutes ) We once again checked the oil level; at this time we observed 15% on the L side quantity. After checking with the QRH  table; We followed as written and continued the flight while monitoring the oil temperature and pressure. During this time the oil temperature was stable and good while the pressure was flickering and slowly dropping (at this time it was still green and within limits). Shortly after this observation we got a 'L ENG OIL PRESS' warning (approximately 3 minutes after initial observation of pressure flickering). We then confirmed the warning and followed QRH. While running through the QRH; We had two of the three specified indications ( L ENG OIL PRESS warning and affected engine oil pressure below limits). We double and triple checked that oil pressure was indeed below limits and referenced the table in the manual. While running the QRH and having pulled back the affected thrust lever to IDLE (QRH); the Left oil pressure was showing 20 PSI (while 25 PSI being the minimum per the manual). We then again quickly saw the pressure dropping again to 19 PSI. We confirmed displayed indications and followed the QRH for an 'Engine Failure/In-Flight Engine Shutdown'. While running the QRH and just before engine shutdown; Left oil pressure was at 19 PSI. while going through the QRH we communicated with ATC and let them know that we were working with an engine issue we than advised ATC once it was clear that an inflight engine shutdown was imminant. We also continued to communicated with dispatch; and Maintenance via ACARS; and informed them of our situation and that we were still planning to continue to ZZZ2 unless thay would suggest otherwise. We continued the flight to ZZZ2 and completed QRH for a SINGLE ENGINE Approach and Landing without any other issues. During the approach bit; we had already set up and briefed for runway XZ into ZZZ2 ( Per ATIS at the time) as we got closer they informed us to expect XA; after receiving this information we communicated amongst ourself and both agreed that runway XZ would be preferred due to its longer length; favoring winds; and reduced workload on us with it already being programmed and briefed I then asked the approach for the current winds in ZZZ2 ( winds were 280 at 7 knots); We then requested XZ and got vectored for the ILS RWY XZ into ZZZ2. Approach and landing were conducted successfully without any further complications. Cause: After reaching the cruising altitude we check the engine oil level and found it to be 15% for the left engine. Shortly after we got a 'L ENG OIL PRESS' warning due to the pressure dropping below limits. During the post flight walk around; I observed leakage on the L ENG exhaust cone (pictures attached).

column121: While accomplishing a-check on gear assignment for Aircraft X found previous improper maintenance done to both wheel well Emdp case drain filters system A and system B for hydraulic case drain filter system servicing done on task card or by Aircraft Maintenance Manual B737ng. For system A the holes were broken on the module and the previous technician installed the safety wire to the adjacent hydraulic line instead of replacing the module and the safety was poorly installed using 20 thousand safety wire. For system B; the previous technician installed the packing that resides inside the module on top of the filter bowl; while correcting the issue; I found the filter not secured to the module because the filter o-rings was installed incorrectly as well not installed in the o-rings slot but sitting on top of the filter; the safety wire was installed loosening and I was able to remove the filter bowl by hand. I corrected both issues by replacing the module and replacing the filters; packings and backup rings. Reference logbook deferral sheet XXXXXXX and XXXXXXY. This is the fifth time in two weeks I have noticed in the wheel well of case drain bowls being safetied to hydraulic lines and second time of the packing being installed on the outside of the bowl and not inside the unit.Cause:  In these instances I was on walkaround while on A-check and pointed it out to the individuals on gear which we corrected these issues; but for Aircraft X; I was on gear and did not have task cards assigned to service these case drain filters. Suggestions:  I feel that the company needs to have a junior mechanic program for individuals who are fresh out of A&P school with no previous experience working at any airline. This is a recipe for disaster and a huge safety hazard. When I started in aviation over XX years ago; we had a ojt program where you were paired with a senior technician and had to accomplish ojt before graduating to the floor. Before arriving at Air Carrier X I worked at the Regional airlines and did contract maintenance heavy jet until I was hired at Air Carrier X. There cannot be inexperienced technicians out on the floor without any prior airline experience with only school under their belt which is the basics. Their should be a minimum of two years mandatory as a junior technician paired up with a senior technician for safety reasons. In the past years with Air Carrier X hiring people fresh out of school; I have seen too many things which can lead to a safety issue; whether the inexperienced individual doesn't ask; doesn't care; or just does a job any type of way without consulting and referencing the aircraft maintenance manual. Something has to be done because I see a huge safety issue and I don't want anything to happen; I am very worried about the lack of experience from people fresh out of school without at least 2 years of hands on experience working at a FBO or airline.                              The low seniority resides on night shift; this is where I feel 85% of the maintenance is being taken place; this is also where new hires mostly fresh out of school are placed due the airlines demand to hire anyone due to the shortage of mechanics and future demands. An airline must hire qualified and experienced technicians or have in place a junior technician program. Since around the time of retiring some of our fleet; the overall workmanship; quality; professionalism of maintaining our aircraft has hugely diminished; this is what I see; this is what a passenger see's as well because our interiors of our aircraft is a reflection of our maintenance program to any passenger that flies on our aircraft.  It is absolutely necessary that a junior program be set in place before senior mechanics with great experience; military experience that has served for this company for over 40 years pass down their knowledge before its too late so that the incoming generation of technicians understand the expectancy level and the requirements of their job qualification as well as performance to be able to provide safety and a quality product to our passengers and the many people we serve across the world. A lot of work is needed in our maintenance program regardless of how much profit we make. In the end; I don't want to hear something on the news and then the company reacts. it will be too late!  I also don't want to see aircraft get damaged or someone get hurt which recently I've seen many close calls. With this being said; we have to do better when it come to safety and quality whether in house or outsourced technicians that provide maintenance to our aircraft.

column121: On Day 0 at XA:45; a mid-air collision nearly occurred between aircraft I was piloting and Aircraft Y. The event occurred on the final approach corridor to Runway 35 at TRM at an estimated distance of 1 mile; and an estimated altitude of 750 feet. The weather was VMC; light winds; clear skies; and unrestricted visibility.Participating Traffic were a small aircraft in left closed traffic for Runway 17 executing a RH 360 on the LH downwind for spacing; another aircraft 6 miles east inbound to Runway 35; a jet holding short of Runway 35 for IFR takeoff. Another jet taxiing from the ramp to Runway 35; Myself in overhead left traffic for Runway 35 having clearly called number 1 for landing during coordination with the small aircraft on the other downwind and the jet holding short for takeoff; and last----Aircraft Y coming straight-in to Runway 35 making distance calls inbound to 'Cochran.' I didn't clearly hear the jet make a radio call. But I don't doubt the word of the other crew at debriefing given the factors described below. In any case; the crew did not recognize that the pattern was full at the airport they were approaching; and they did not coordinate their plan to come straight-in with any of the other aircraft using the airport.As I was descending from base to final; I was a bit high on approach. I received a TCAS TA while turning final. After rolling out on final the displayed threat aircraft was 100 feet directly beneath me (solid-yellow circle -100).No TCAS RA was issued since both aircraft were configured for landing below 1000 feet. This situation was something like a perfect storm that somewhat defanged the TCAS. Since the initial TA showed yellow and stayed yellow (20-48 seconds); the urgency of the situation was confused; and my initial reflex was to think that there was another aircraft in the vicinity of the airport; but not one on approach. It took me a moment after establishing myself on final to note that the threat symbol; and myself were collocated on the TCAS screen with only 100 feet of separation.Since I did not have full SA or visual contact with the threat aircraft; I was sufficiently confused by the situation to abandon the approach. I executed a go-around and re-entered the left downwind as Aircraft Y landed and rolled out on the runway.A second approach was safely completed without incident.All local traffic were coordinating using the phrase 'Thermal area traffic' to identify the airport and operations. This is normal at this airport even though the airport is called 'Jaqueline Cochrane Regional' airport. The word Thermal contains 2 syllables. The official name of the airport contains 7. This CTAF frequency is often very congested due to the uncontrolled traffic volume at this airport. It was congested at the time of this event.The crew was unfamiliar(first-time to the airport); and did not associate 'Thermal' with the airport they were landing at. As a consequence; they didn't participate in coordination efforts with the other aircraft using the airport. They rightly pointed out on debriefing that 'Thermal' is not printed on any of the airport plates. Thus; local habituated knowledge and telephony understandably contributed to all affected crews' loss of SA.Also a contributing factor was the inhibition of a TCAS RA at low altitude. The yellow-circle symbol did not reflexively indicate the proximate danger present during this event. Even so; without the TA advisory; I am confident that a catastrophic collision would have occurred. This can go up as a TCAS save----if a somewhat confusing one.The traffic situation surrounding this event; and every day at this airport during the snow-bird season can produce a situational-picture that is way too much for any single-pilot in a jet to safely keep track of. I'm a pilot not an air-traffic controller.At 100 feet of vertical separation; and no visual contact made; this was a very close call. This is my second traffic related go-around at this airport in X years due to jet-aircraft coming straight-in to a full-pattern without participating in effective self-coordination.This airport needs an Air Traffic Control Tower----like yesterday!

column121: I had a flight scheduled with a student pilot. The plane was Aircraft X. We both completed a preflight and had a full tank of fuel. Everything seemed normal. We taxied to the runway at ZZZ1 and did our run up. The magnetos showed around 50rpm drop each; as expected. Fuel pressure was normal; oil pressure was in the green arc. Everything was looking normal. We were cleared for takeoff on runway XX and my student applied full throttle rapidly. Immediately we both felt a sputter in the engine and I called for an aborted takeoff. We exited the runway on taxiway 1 and returned to the run up area. I wanted to try to diagnose the issue. I triple checked everything and went through the run up checklist another time. I completed a fouled spark plug checklist just in case that was the issue but I did not believe it was. I concluded that the sputter was due to the aggressive application of the throttle. We agreed to attempt the takeoff again with a smoother application of the throttle but if there was any sign of an issue; we would cancel and taxi back. The second attempt was normal and the engine had no issue so we took off. We took off. The rest of the flight was uneventful. We stayed on flight following while we did a cross country to ZZZ with the plan to return to ZZZ1 after. Based on traffic and our direction of flight; we elected to do a straight in for runway XY. We started our descent checklist and began descending to pattern altitude. We transferred over the ZZZ [CTAF] and began announcing our position. When we had just passed a 1 mile final; we were a little low for the approach and I instructed my student to add more power. I looked at her hand and noticed she had already added power but we weren't getting much power out of the engine. I didn't look at the tachometer but could tell based on the sound that we did not have a high RPM. Additionally; we were not gaining altitude and were still descending. I realized we had an issue and immediately say 'my controls' while trying to do quick troubleshooting. I checked the mixture and the fuel pump were both full rich and turned on. I attempted different throttle settings but had no change in RPM and heard more sputtering in the engine. I hadn't heard this before on this flight but sounded similar to when we aborted takeoff. The engine was still making noise and the propeller was still spinning but we had a partial power loss and would not be able to make it to the runway. At this point we were descending toward trees. I made a right turn for a field and did a soft field landing in this field. There was not more than 30 seconds from telling my student to add throttle and then landing in the field. There was no damage to person; property; or aircraft.

column121: I left ZZZ1 at approximately XA:30 on Day 0 on an IFR flight plan and was cleared on route direct to ZZZ. I was the sole occupant of the airplane. I climbed to 16;000 feet and the flight was very normal. Approximately 50 miles from ZZZ I was turned over to ZZZ Approach and requested the RNAV XX via ZZZZZ IAF. The most recent METAR had 3 knot winds that equaled a 2 knot tail wind but I elected to land on Runway XX because the landing roll would be shorter due to the upslope. My approach and approach speed were very normal and at 500 feet I confirmed that I met all of my stable approach criteria. The most recent FICON was 100% 1/8' dry snow 5/5/5.My airspeed was approximately 85 kts. when I started to flare. My flaps were at 20 degrees I had three green landing gear indicators. I had a very smooth touchdown just after the PAPI. The runway markings were obscured by snow but I landed on or very near the center line. I touched down first on the main landing gear and when the nose gear touched down; the nose veered left. I attempted to correct this with right rudder. The airplane began to fishtail and I continued to try to correct with rudder. After a couple of attempts to correct; the fishtails became worse and I attempted to initiate a go-around. At that time my right main landing gear caught the edge of the snow on the right side of the runway which caused the airplane to turn to the right and exit the runway into the snow. The snow caused the nose gear to collapse which caused a prop strike. I was not injured in any way.

column121: Yesterday shortly after takeoff from ZZZ we had what I was told by the purser was a near miss. Meaning the pilots had to abruptly pull upwards in order to avoid being hit by another aircraft. We were still seated due to turbulence but we had already passed 10;000 ft because the purser was in the middle of his announcements when this happened. I remember myself and the other flight attendant in the back looked at each other in shock and held onto our jump seats. It felt like a roller coaster almost so we automatically knew it wasn't turbulence. It felt like when you are driving and have to swerve quickly in order to avoid hitting something/being hit. The pilots pulled upwards bringing the aircraft higher in such a quick manner that we were instantly concerned. After finishing the inflight service announcements the purser called us and asked if we all felt that and if we were okay. We told him yes we felt it and luckily we were all still seated so we were physically okay. Later on towards the end of the flight the purser came back and told us that during a lavatory break the Captain had told him that we had a near miss with another aircraft and that's why they had pulled up like that so abruptly. The Captain also told him not to mention anything in front of the passengers. The purser then told us not to say anything to anyone and to keep it between ourselves/the crew. We were both stunned and couldn't believe what we were hearing. After landing I was expecting the pilots to at least debrief us since all passengers had deplaned and we were keeping the aircraft for our return flight to ZZZ but they did not. I even waited in first class for them to open the flight deck and come out to and talk to us but they never did. I was still in shock and shaken up so I just went to the lavatory in the back and just cried. I was so scared and feeling so many emotions and didn't want anyone else to see me cry. I am grateful that the pilots were able to get us there safely but it was off putting when nothing was said about the incident after the flight. It does not make me feel safe or comfortable knowing what happened and not being able to discuss it with the pilots after the fact.

When I got to the stop sign and I realized that I had only driven a couple miles and I'm looking at equipment behind a fence. I know something isn't right. column121: Aircraft X was dispatched with MEL 28XXX for the #2 spar valve light; which stayed bright (indicating 'in transit') when the cutoff lever was moved to cutoff. I've had several deferred valve lights recently; this one caught my attention. The MEL allows dispatch but requires a mechanic to verify operation of the actual valve 1x/day. I called the dispatcher; who patched in maintenance control then the Chief Pilot and a Lead Mechanic. None was able to give greater technical insight than my ground-school understanding of the fuel feed system. All of them reasoned that Boeing; the FAA; Air Carrier X; and the union have all signed off on this deferral; and the chances of the valve failing to begin with are pretty small; not zero; but small. With all due respect; no one disagreed with my concern; that just because the valve worked when a mechanic checked it doesn't mean it will work now - and while that is always the case; the lack of an indicator light could lead; in the event of an engine fire; to the possibility of the loss of redundant shutoff valves between the fuel tanks and the burning engine. Not having that information during an emergency could cost the pilots critically. I accepted the aircraft; but in retrospect; not being able to verify the position of the valve seems like unnecessary risk. The analogy I offered is that I would not accept an aircraft with no gear-down indicator light even if the mechanics verified operation of the gear down-locks before every flight. Sure; the valve probably won't fail; and the gear will probably come down; not being able to verify it is the problem. Our first mandate is safety. Everything else comes after.

column121: Inbound aircraft arrived at gate XX later than scheduled.  Flight crew prepared aircraft for departure in a timely fashion.  Upon making contact with ramp agent via interphone; the ramp agent sounded agitated and spoke in a rushed manner.  Ramp agent requested the flight crew to 'release brake we need to reset something'.  CA said 'parking brake released' and released the brake.  The aircraft was not chocked and started to move.  CA immediately reapplied the parking brake.  The movement prompted the CA to query the ramp agent regarding whether or not the aircraft was captured.  The Ramp agent responded by saying 'Sorry it was not captured it is slippery outside' .  The ground crew then removed an apparently disabled tug from the safety area and pushed the aircraft normally with a new tug.Cause: During this event; I was heads down as I had accidentally entered the operations frequency twice in the standby and needed to relocate the correct ramp frequency.  Due to the fact that I split my attention between this task and listening to the ramp conversation; I did not catch all the details which reduced my situational awareness and ability to back up the captain.  The ramp agent was somewhat difficult to understand; was rushing to replace the disabled tug; and did not give any reason for the brake release instruction that would have caused the flight crew to question if the aircraft was secured.  The ramp agent requested that the captain release the parking brake when the aircraft was not otherwise secured; likely due to pressure for an on-time departure.Suggestions: In the future;  I will question thoroughly any instructions from ground crew to release the parking brake for any non-standard reason.  I will make sure the captain verifies with the ground crew that the aircraft is secured prior to any non-standard brake release instructions.
column123: Departing gate XX in ORD; aircraft was ready for block out. Flight crew called ground personnel ready for brake release. Ground informed flight crew they were ready but our tug died so we'll have you release the brake then reset it; and we'll hook up the other tug." Captain released the brake getting an out time 1 minute early; then reset brake. During this release the aircraft rolled back approximately 2-3 feet as the aircraft was on a downslope and the tug was never connected; this is the only aircraft movement of the entire event. Flight crew queried the ground personnel as to why the aircraft rolled and were informed ground personnel did not connect tug because "it's slippery with de-ice fluid on the ground." The second tug was then connected and push commenced as normal. Cause: Multiple causes of this event contributed to the roll. First cause is captain being complacent and trusting ground personnel instead of verifying the ground crew connected the tug. Second cause is the operational pressures put on employees to always get flights out on time; if this pressure was less the second tug would have been connected a minute or so after scheduled departure but this roll would not have occurred. Third cause is the operational norm of the ground personnel that ask for brake release quite often when they are not fully ready so the flight will not take a delay. Suggestions: As captain I always should be verifying all actions are done in the correct way and not allow the aircraft to move unless it is in the safest way possible. Ground crew should also verify the aircraft is in a safe state before asking for any brake releases and have a tug hooked."

column121: Preflight; start; taxi; takeoff; departure and enroute phases were uneventful. On the ZZZZZ Arrival to Runway XXL at ZZZZ; while descending through approximately Flight Level (FL)180; an AUTOTHROTTLE DISCREPANCY EICAS message was displayed. The auto-throttles became inoperative and did not reset.Shortly thereafter; at approximately FL170; a THRUST ASYM COMPENSATION EICAS message appeared. The THRUST ASYM COMPENSATION checklist was completed and appeared to reset the system; however; the auto-throttles remained inoperative.At approximately FL160; the THRUST ASYM COMPENSATION message returned. Within a few seconds; the aircraft began rolling left and right up to approximately 30 degrees of bank. The Captain (PF) disconnected the autopilot in an attempt to arrest the roll oscillations. Despite opposite control inputs and autopilot disconnection; the aircraft continued rolling for approximately 2-3 oscillations before returning to wings level. The THRUST ASYM COMPENSATION message would not reset again.Approaching the ZZZ [VOR] hold at approximately FL110; the autopilot was re-engaged. The aircraft appeared to respond normally; with the exception of the auto-throttles. FLCH mode and 220 knots were selected and indicated normally.Shortly after leveling at FL100; the aircraft again began oscillating in roll. No yaw oscillation was observed. The autopilot was disconnected; however; the aircraft continued to oscillate and did not immediately respond to pilot control inputs for several oscillations. The flight control diagnostic page was selected. Control surface indications corresponded with the roll oscillations; and no rudder movement was observed. After approximately 2-3 additional oscillations; full manual control was regained and the aircraft returned to level flight.Approximately 5 NM prior to entering the ZZZ [VOR] hold; the Captain (PF) directed the First Officer (PM) to notify ATC and request priority handling for an approach to RWY XXL at ZZZZ.While descending through FL90; all Mode Control Panel (MCP) modes appeared to become inoperative. No modes could be activated. No mode indicator lights were on. At approximately 5;000 feet; on an 14-mile base leg for RWY XXL; MCP functionality appeared to return. LOC capture and APPROACH mode functioned normally. Auto-throttles became available and functioned normally through landing.A normal landing was accomplished. Ground control directed the aircraft to stop on taxiway 1 and contact Emergency Services. While stopped on the taxiway. The FO transmitted that no additional assistance was required. The aircraft taxied normally to the assigned gate and was shut down without further incident.Causal Factors are unknown at this time; without additional information from maintenance post-flight data from the aircraft.

column121: On descent into ZZZ while being vectored to the downwind for runway XX; we received a WING ANTI/ICE fail". We were in IMC with an OAT of between 0 to 3 degrees Celsius. I continued to fly the aircraft and I instructed the FO to run the QRH; as he had stated he flew this aircraft last week and had the same issue. After selecting the ice detector override knob to "all" and I advanced the thrust; the caution went away for approximately 60 seconds. Upon the caution's return we continued the next steps of the QRH and the I advocated to request priority handling. We quickly agreed as a crew and requested priority handling with ZZZ [TRACON] approach control to allow us to receive priority in exiting icing conditions and so I could have the ability to request whatever I thought we needed to safely arrive in ZZZ; as well as having a failure of an aircraft system. The next QRH step required us to push out then push in the wing anti ice button. The caution disappeared for approximately 60 seconds before returning. At this point; I decided we couldn't rely on the indication and to run the QRH as though the message persists. We requested minimum vectoring altitude and a wider base to final from ATC to avoid icing conditions and remain within QRH limitations of 30 degrees of bank and 190 minimum airspeed for flaps 0 and 9 degrees. After transmitting this request the caution went away. We were on our final vector for final when it returned. We agreed that there was no ice accumulation to warrant the "ice accretion" steps and we continued with the approach. Around this time; I had my FO notify dispatch. Due to the possibility of icing; I did not delay the approach and talk to the flight attendant; as we were already below 10;000' and we were more focused on getting the aircraft on the ground.The airport did set up priority handling vehicles as a precaution; and the FO gave them all pertinent information while I contacted maintenance.We landed without incident. My FO did a walk around and noticed no visible signs of damage to the leading wing edges on his post flight inspection.Honestly; maintenance should have had the Captain write it up on the date when my FO had this issue the last time and we wouldn't have had an issue on this day.It sounded like; from the FO's recollection; this aircraft had this issue before with the same aircraft in moderate icing. When his Captain called maintenance after the flight; maintenance convinced him one way or another to not write the airplane up. When I called maintenance; they said I didn't have enough pressure and even though the temperature shows in the green on the Environmental Control System; page; it doesn't mean there's enough pressure. I understand this concept; but I was flaps 9 doing 240kts. column123: On descent into ZZZ while being vectored to the downwind for runway XX; we received a WING ANTI/ICE fail". We were in IMC with an OAT of 3 degrees Celsius. I called in and stated the altitude I was leaving; the altitude I was climbing to and that I was on a heading of 035. The controller then stated that he had a low altitude warning to turn to a northwesterly heading and to climb immediately to 3000 feet. I complied and looked out the window and tried to determine where the terrain was. I also later looked at the chart to see if there was some tall structure that could cause the warning there was none. I continued to step climb on headings with the controller.I talked with PHX Approach. He never stated that any separation was lost with any other aircraft and while I was flying; I did not ever see on ADSB or visually any other traffic. I did state that I wanted the tapes at GEU Tower. He stated he could not do that. I said you can't get the tapes at GEU; he said he couldn't. I said I should call GEU and he said I would have to file some special govt paperwork request to get them. I of course wanted the tapes to verify what heading the Tower had told me to fly. He then asked why I turned to the heading that I did. I said because that is the heading the Tower gave me. Basically; he was not going to do anything to get the tapes at GEU Tower. I also stated that this had been my first time IFR out of GEU; that I had never gotten clearance to the north on an IFR departure and that I had never departed even VFR to the north. I stated if I had; I may had recognized if this was not a typical heading. I had nothing to compare it with any other departure; if it may have been an incorrect heading. I also stated that when the GEU Controller had been worried about which direction I was going at the end of the runway; it would have been more helpful to hear from the controller something like 'Verify turning to heading such and such. This would have given a better check to the assigned heading.I stated that I had been startled when the controller gave the low altitude alert; he stated so was the controller. I asked where the terrain was? He stated that it most likely broke a MVA. He started to explain how a controller had to open an area for a heading if it is to be used. As I said before I looked at the charts closely later and did not see any high structures.Other circumstances: Glendale is a very busy airport with traffic. Did the controller or I mix up the numbers. Did the relay from PHX Departure give Tower the wrong heading or is there a standard heading that is always given for that area of departure. I don't know; but it seems nobody wants me to hear the GEU Tower tapes

column121: Flight was normal and vectors to ILS XXL was programmed into the FMS as usual. The flight was vectored to final and intercepted the final approach course.  The crew was advised to maintain 3000 until ZZZZZ which is 9 miles from the XXL threshold. Normally the Proline 21 avionics automatically switches from long range nav (pink needles) to short range (green needles); but for some reason this did not occur when expected.  Because vectors to final was selected; only ZZZZZ1(point prior to the FAF) and subsequent fixes were displayed on the moving map.  The FMS generated glidepath came down and the Captain asked why the autopilot did not intercept the glidepath.  He then initiated a descent to capture the glidepath.  Shortly after; the tower called with a low altitude warning and a go around was initiated.  We were vectored around for another approach and landing which was uneventful. I as the non-flying pilot knew something was wrong but could not determine what was causing my confusion.  Both pilots lost situational awareness regarding our exact position ultimately as a result of selecting vectors to final.Neither pilot referred to the moving map display on their ipads and neither pilot looked  at the standby Horizontal Situation Indicator which was presenting ILS information.  Even more importantly; DME position was not compared to the approach chart.There were several lessons learned from this experience. Always program the full approach so that all points on the approach will be displayed on the map. Don't depend on cockpit automation.  Manually select short range nav if this information is needed  before automatic switching occurs.Always use any available information to ascertain position.  Bottom line; get back to the basics and listen to that uneasy feeling.  Don't continue a bad approach.

column121: On Day 0 at approximately XA:30; IP Person A and student Person B were inbound to land at Mankato (MKT) from a flight lesson in ZZZ; flying in Aircraft X. Runway 33 was the active; and we had entered the pattern via a midfield cross. Flying the pattern was uneventful until the final leg.As we turned on final; my student made a radio call stating our position. We had traffic in sight (Aircraft Y) that was holding short of Runway 33. It was a calm and clear day so our groundspeed was probably around 70-80 kts. We heard Aircraft Y make a call stating that they were departing on Runway 33. In my mind I thought 'Wow that's cutting it close but they could probably make it'; but then; I didn't see the aircraft roll across the hold short line after making their departure call. I then thought 'Maybe they just now saw us on final and are waiting for us to land'; but I still maintained vigilance that they might depart anyways. Right after I had that thought; they rolled past the threshold line onto the runway for takeoff. By that time we were less than a mile on final. I had Person B stay on the controls and fly the plane while I watched the traffic outside. We saw them start their roll; but determined we would not be able to land safely without creating an incursion; so we executed a go around. We side-stepped to ther right to avoid catching up to or overflying the departure traffic; but could only side-step so much as there was other traffic on the upwind leg of the pattern (Mankato has an upwind leg for traffic sequencing reasons). At one point we were only separated by 100 feet; and I could no longer maintain visual contact with Aircraft Y due to our nose-up attitude for the go around and our spacing being so close. I'm not sure what our altitude was when we executed the go-around; as I was keeping my eyes outside watching for traffic.As soon as it was safe to do so; my student and I opted to break out of the pattern rather than turning crossdwind in order to recollect and re-assess the situation. When we landed; we each submitted a safety report. We also discussed the situation and determined that we had the right of way. We agreed that something we could have done better was make the go around decision sooner; which would have provided better spacing.

column121: While operating a Part 135 charter flight in Aircraft X at SFO; we were instructed to taxi from the ramp to Runway 1R. Ground Control issued progressive taxi instructions; however; due to frequency congestion and perceived pressure from the controller to expedite movement; the taxi clearance was delivered rapidly.The airport surface environment at SFO is complex; with numerous closely spaced and angled intersections. Taxiway markings in the area appeared faded and were difficult to distinguish; particularly at high-workload intersections. Signage and painted surface identifiers did not provide clear situational awareness in the moment.While attempting to comply promptly with ATC instructions and maintain flow; we inadvertently taxied onto the incorrect taxiway at one of the intersections. The error was recognized shortly thereafter through cross-checking the airport diagram and outside visual cues. We immediately corrected course and notified Ground Control. No loss of separation or runway incursion occurred.Contributing factors included: Complex taxiway layout at SFO. Faded or unclear taxiway markings. High workload during taxi phase. Congested frequency. Perceived ATC pressure to expedite. Time pressure associated with Part 135 operations. Crew resource management was utilized to identify and correct the deviation promptly. After recognizing uncertainty; we slowed the aircraft and verified position using the airport diagram before proceeding.Human Factors: Time pressure. Communication workload. Expectation bias. Reduced situational awareness due to environmental complexity.Corrective Actions / Recommendations: When operating at complex airports such as SFO; request progressive taxi instructions early and advise ATC if unable to comply promptly. Reduce taxi speed in high-density ramp and intersection areas. If any uncertainty exists; stop the aircraft and clarify position before proceeding. Airport authority should evaluate taxiway marking visibility and signage clarity in the departure areas.

I then switched Aircraft Y to the radar controller about a half mile off of the departure end of runway XX on a 150 heading. After both aircraft were switched to the radar controller's frequency I observed Aircraft X; who was at this point about 2 miles south of the runway; turn directly towards Aircraft Y with targets appearing likely to merge at co-altitude. Ultimately; a 170 heading was coordinated in the rundown for Aircraft Y and another more eastbound heading of 150 was coordinated and approved by the radar controller. The radar controller decided to turn Aircraft X directly towards Aircraft Y creating a near mid air collision. Lastly; I think that it is worth noting that the radar controller is a supervisor who is certified only in one position in the facility and received that certification with zero recommendations from a CPC in the building. I would like to recommend that all those in training whether they are developmentals or supervisors be required to receive a recommendation from a CPC before they are considered for certification.

column121: This aircraft had a L engine exceedance and engine swap prior to report time. This was the first flight after engine change with a MEL deferral It required an ETOPs verification flight (1 hour cruise; all systems normal per FOM 5.60.2) before legal to enter the ETOPs area of operation.  Showing at aircraft about an hour before departure; three Maintenance personnel were working in the cockpit.  The crew gained cockpit access around the departure time. After a few maintenance issues were resolved on the ground (L thrust REV status message; Auto Spoiler EICAS; and previous exceedance that wasn't cleared); we pushed about an hour late.  All was normal until takeoff roll.  Around 80-100 knts; the left engine N1 vibration indicator was higher than normal and the box inverted to white with black digits in the 4.0 range.  Takeoff was continued (no EICAS indications) and vibrations weren't felt on the throttle and airframe until past the low-speed abort phase and into initial climb. One of the Relief Pilots also thought he smelled something not normal.  The FO noted an additional vibration surge above 5.0 occurred during power reduction at 1500 AGL. The non-normal engine indications made ETOPs entry illegal; so the decision was to hold over water and dump 200;000 lbs. of fuel or land overweight   Dumping fuel would delay landing an additional 45 minutes.  AAs the engine was not working normally on its first flight; I decided landing overweight to be the safer option to get on the ground sooner with long runways available back in ZZZ.  This had been coordinated previously with dispatch regarding the ETOPs verification options.  After initial climb out; we completed the After Takeoff checklist as I wanted to clean up and get some altitude to discuss the issue.  The crew concurred to return to ZZZ per our plan with Dispatch on the ETOPs verification.We requested a level off with ATC and were assigned 14;000MSL on the ZZZZZ SID; then a request to return to ZZZ.  ATC cleared us direct ZZZ and descent to 11;000 MSL and to expect the ILS XXR.  While I (PF) and the FO (PM) prepared for the approach; the Relief Pilots assisted by getting a SATCOM with Dispatch.  I had them inform the FAs and Passengers of our plan to return to ZZZ.  We run the electronic Overweight Landing checklist and determined we had to use Flaps 25 for landing as the target speed was over 161KTS.  I believe the final target speed was 167KTS.  The FO pulled up ACARs landing data for RWY XXR that we knew was slightly longer than the takeoff RWY XXL.   Brakes 4 selected.  Approach was brief and Descent checklist completed.  ATC vectored us similar to a ZZZZZ1 STAR down the bay as we slowed and descended.   The approach was uneventful on the ILS to XXR.  Landing checklist and callouts per SOP.  Touchdown was smooth rolling to the end and exiting RWY XXR.  After crossing XXL on Taxiway 1; the brake temps began to increase; so we coordinated with ground to hold on taxiway 1 and have the ear inspected for hot brakes.  APU was started and engines shutdown to allow the parking brake to be released with no aircraft movement.  Brakes began to cool and we verified no fire or fuse plug issues from fire rescue vehicles. We requested to be towed back to gate to avoid using brakes or need to restart engines. After the brakes had cooled around 30 min and began going from amber back to normal; Maintenance and tug crews connected and towed aircraft back to gate XX.  Normal checklists completed at gate and passengers deplaned.  Maintenance write-ups for the engine vibration experienced on the left engine and the BRAKE TEMP EICAS.

I reset the appropriate altitude in the MCP and the rest of the approach was uneventful. Lessens learned are taking more time in holding to prepare for approach; verifying what you see; and use of VNAV.
