column121: A series of systems failures led to an engine fire shortly after takeoff.Just after raising the landing gear after lift off we; the crew; heard and felt a vibration that was very much like a nose wheel rubbing on the scrubbers; and we smelled what we thought was burnt rubber.  We all thought that a nose tire had perhaps failed and was disintegrating against the scrubbers.   Each of us had experienced this before.  However; this vibration went on too long.  At this point we were at around 1000 AFE and the #2 hydraulic system lost all quantity.The #2 hydraulic system lost all quantity to the standpipe level; but we still had hydraulic pressure.  I decided to wait until we were in a lower threat phase of flight to deal with this issue.  We were perhaps now at 1500 AFE and I noticed that the #2 engine vibration was very high.  I called this out to the crew.  I don't remember the exact number.  All other engine indications were normal; and the N1 and EGT matched the other engines (as far as I can recall). Then; the #2 engine failed. The Relief Pilot called out #2 engine failure.  I decided to run the engine failure checklist.  The FO advised me to wait until flaps were up.  This is the correct procedure following a V1 cut; but I felt that in this case we were high enough to begin the checklist.  However; I agreed to the FO's suggestion.  At this point we were probably 2000 AFE.  I notified ATC and the engine caught fire. The #2 engine caught fire and I ran the fire checklist while the FO flew.  At this point the vibration was gone and we knew what the problem actually was.  The fire went out after the first fire bottle.I now took over pilot flying duties.  We returned to ZZZZ for a landing and the fire department checked the aircraft while we were on the runway.  The fire was out and we had the necessary hydraulics to taxi back to the ramp so we taxied back and shut down.Maintenance later showed me that we had multiple bird strikes all over the aircraft and much damage as a result; including a hole in the right wing root.Perhaps I could have ran the severe engine damage checklist before the engine failed.  However; all engine indications except the vibration were normal.  I would have expected a high EGT; surging N1 and banging noises if we had severe engine damage; and we had none of these.
column123: Upon gear retraction; we heard what we thought was nose gear scrubbing. The sound persisted; and grew louder; and we even commented how none of us had ever had a nose gear make that sound for that long. We then smelled what we thought was burning rubber. Passing through 1500; we got engine vibrations indications on the EICAS engine display. Shortly after; HYD QTY 2 LO caution alert. As Relief Pilot; I kept an eye on number 2 engine indicator; and shortly after called out that #2 was rolling back. We then got ENGINE 2 FAIL alert. Captain notified ATC; called for checklist; but FO (PF) recommended we wait until cleanup. Capt agreed. Shortly after; we received OVHT ENGINE 2 NAC; then subsequent FIRE ENGINE 2. At this time; we were around 3500; climbing to 4000; and decided to run Engine fire 2 checklist. We reported engine failure with ATC; and began immediate vectors back to ZZZZ for an approach to RWY XXL. Being below max landing weight; we had no concerns with the relatively quick vectors; Captain and FO ran checklists and set up the FMS; I ran landing performance; and we reported to ATC our information and Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) requirements. Still suspecting nose gear and hydraulic issues causing the fire; we discussed stopping on the runway for inspection. Capt flew the approach; and we landed uneventfully. We stopped on the runway; ARFF trucks inspected and saw no further damage or fire; and we opted to taxi to parking under power. Upon parking; maintenance teams discovered significant bird evidence and damage. We had discussed birds during the CRM/threat briefing. However; suggestions the future include caution against confirmation bias. The timing of the vibrations and noise were perfectly coincident with what we thought was a nose gear spinning in the wheel well; and further confirmation bias from what we thought was burning rubber. Aside from that; we all acknowledged external factors; such as the recent similar accident; caused a little extra stress that might not otherwise exist. However; this incident certainly cemented the importance of having a full crew; as we all worked together and each was able to contribute to bringing the event to a safe conclusion.

column121: During transition into DFW from FL310 we executed the appropriate 'Descent Checklist' and set the altimeters to 30.57. Throughout the arrival there was no indication of error from ATC. Upon reaching DELMO at what we believed to be 12;000 MSL we were given a frequency change to 118.42 and instructed to continue our descent to 6000 MSL. During the descent we were instructed to expedite and given additional clearances to 5000msl while turning base; 4000 MSL on base; and 3000 MSL on base to final. While rolling out on a 160 heading to intercept the 18R LOC for the visual approach. ATC asked us to verify our altitude. At this point we were still descending to 3000 MSL indicated. ATC then verified the altimeter setting of 29.57 and instructed us to level at 2300 MSL. Nearly simultaneously ATC issued a 'low altitude alert'. I immediately disengaged the Auto Pilot and pitched slightly nose high to level and reduce speed from 210 kts. While maneuvering the aircraft the  PM was able to get the appropriate altimeter setting and we were able to use his PFD (Primary Flight Display) to verify altitude. Once acceptable altitude and heading for the approach was achieved I was able to set my altimeter to the appropriate setting and proceed with a stable approach to landing. Cause: Multiple factors contributed to causing this incident. Pilot complacency with higher altimeter settings associated with cooler climate therefore not being alerted to the significant change when arriving in a warmer environment. Misinterpretation of the ATIS altimeter setting; failure to verify the altimeter setting; and lastly a lack of warning from ATC that previous altitude restrictions at altitude had been missed by nearly 1;000 MSL. Suggestions: Apply common sense when returning to warmer climates after conducting consecutive operations in cooler weather.
column123: When descending on the boove7 into DFW passing 18k we set the wrong altimeter setting. 30.57 instead of 29.57. We descended down to 12k indicated with approach and when handed off told to descend to 6k and expedite. We continued to descend and were told to continue down to 5k and turn 15 degrees right eventually. We continuously descended from 12k towards our final cleared altitude of 3k as we turned final. Approach asked if we were going down to 2300 because we were cleared to 3000 and I replied were at approx 3300 going to 3k. ATC responded we were already below that and gave us the correct altimeter setting. Fo flying disengaged autopilot to stop descent and begin climbing. We reset the altimeter to the correct setting and were cleared for the approach and handed to tower. FO continued to hand fly the visual to landing. Cause: Usually an altimeter that high would cause a second glance but with this weeks cold front that had been a typical setting. Checking the ATIS against the setting an additional time would have also caught the error. Our printer was having clarity issues and we read our takeoff v speeds off our EFB to verify they were correct due to a misprint. ATC never noticed or alerted us that we had been low on the arrival even when leveling off at the bottom altitude then we were given a continuous descent down until the lower than assigned altitude was noticed. When approach gave us the altimeter on initial contact it wasn't noticed that it was different than what we had set. Suggestions: Double check the ATIS printout more regularly and if ATC notices an aircraft below the level off final altitude it is indicative of an incorrect altimeter setting.

UTC clocks; terrain displays; and Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) also ceased operation. To mitigate the loss of navigation performance; we requested to shoot a VOR approach to a runway that would keep us over the city of El Paso and away from terrain. This allowed us to navigate to a position to get visual contact of the runway and perform a visual approach. Upon landing some GPS functionality started to return such as terrain displays and the FO's clock.Caused by the military doing broad and unannounced jamming operations. Either the military adequately warns of such activity or cease them all together. Disruption of civilian air traffic into terrain sensitive airports is not acceptable.

column121: We were in constant contact with Dispatch throughout the flight to APN about the weather and runway conditions. While in route the first report was 2/2/2 with 3 inches of wet snow on the runway of intended use. We were informed that they were currently working on the runway to improve conditions. We continued the flight to the IAF and held over JEGOB while we awaited the newest update. 5 minutes before bingo fuel the report came in as 3/3/3 with 1/4-inch dry compacted snow. So with the weather still being about minimums we began the approach and made a landing. In was night so it was impossible for us to tell the actual runway conditions until after touchdown and on roll out when we discovered the braking action was NIL and there was at least 1 inch of visible snow on the surface. With full thrust reverse almost any application of the brakes cause the airplane to slide on the runway. We managed to eventually slow the aircraft and had to come to a complete stop before attempting to turn off at the very end of the runway but still slid a great deal while attempting the turn. Taxiing very slowing back to the gate the taxiways were no better causing us to slide with any attempt to slow the aircraft. Out of safety concerns we did not operate the flight back to ZZZ that night.The next day we returned to the airport to attempt to return to ZZZ. The trucks worked on the runway conditions for several hours and the reported to us 3/3/3 with 1/8-inch dry compacted snow. After the events of the previous evening we asked if they would take us out to see the runway conditions for ourselves. It was at the time we discovered that it was 1/8-inch or more of 100% ice with 1/8-inch or more snow on top over the entire runway surface. The truck taking us to the runway slide every time doing a brake check going only 20 mph. He allowed us to get out the truck and confirm it was ice which was difficult to even walk on. The ice was obvious yet the station did not want to report it.Cause: The airport not accurately reporting the runway conditions.Suggestions: Audit the airport and their runway condition reporting procedures.

column121: ZZZ - AGS. Upon landing in AGS on Runway 17 at approximately XA:00; we slowed to make our taxi off at the end of the runway onto Taxiway Foxtrot. It was difficult to identify a taxiway lead-off line as it was not painted entirely onto the runway. Additionally; because of airport construction there appeared to be an extra piece of pavement prior to Taxiway Foxtrot that was not accurately depicted on the airport diagram. Due to this misinterpretation and dark conditions; my Captain preemptively made the turn onto the additional concrete before the taxiway. We both realized that we had initiated the turn too early and immediately came to a stop. We explained to Tower that we had made the turn too early but were still on the runway. In communication with Tower; we attempted to make a 180-degree turn to get ourselves back into a position to enter the taxiway. However; the taxiway lights were positioned into the runway and prevented us from making a turn. My Captain then attempted to make a turn in the other direction. However; I had to ask him to stop as one of the runway marking signs was in the way of our expected path. We decided as a crew that it was best to come to a stop and have a tug come out to push us back. Tower helped us to coordinate with Operations to have a tug enter the runway and assist in pushing us back. Communication was made with the passengers and flight attendants before the tug pushed us back about 20 feet. This was enough for us to then disconnect and move under our own power. We then back-taxied down the runway and finally to our gate.Cause: I think both my Captain and I could have done a better job of confidently identifying the taxiway before making the turn using the taxiway lights as cues. Overall; I believe the cause of the mistake was the lack of markings and mapping of this additional pavement caused by the ongoing construction. Once we had initiated this turn; there was no way of straightening back out to correct the mistake as the taxiway lights protruded far into the runway and the runway marking sign impeded our path in the other direction.
column123: Upon landing on Runway 17; we rolled to the end to get off runway. As we made the turn we realized we were not on taxiway; but rather some piece of pavement next to taxiway. We stopped the aircraft and told Tower our situation. They called Operations out with a tug. Once pushed back we taxied to gate.Cause: The taxiway diagram was not correct. Multiple construction vehicles still working.

column121: While operating as PIC from FAR to ZZZ; we prepared for push. We had good communications with ramp crew. During pushback; we were cleared to start engines. My FO started the right engine. The push crew pushed us; stopped; and continued the push several times. I had been told my previous trip to Fargo that they were still creating the proper procedures to push aircraft off of the new gates; so we attributed the several stops to the push crew being unfamiliar with the new area and push procedures.At one point; we stopped for a longer period of time. I asked the push operator if we were complete with the push; but got no response. I then noticed we seemed to be moving forward. I asked why we were moving forward and got no response. I looked further down below the nose while trying to determine why we were getting no response and saw what looked like people working near the nosewheel while my FO announced that we were definitely moving forwards.I chose to slam on the brakes to avoid possibly running over the ground grew who appeared to be near the nosewheel. I then told the tug operator to stop everything and tell me what was going on before we continued. He informed me that they had disconnected my aircraft from the tug without telling us or asking for the brakes to be set. After reminding them that communicating this with the crew was a vital safety measure; the tug operator apologized for forgetting and admitted it was his first time pushing an aircraft. There was no training supervisor present.Fortunately; my FO and I were paying attention during the push and I was able to stop the aircraft and prevent anybody from being hurt or any equipment from being damaged.This incident reinforced to our crew the importance of keeping high situational awareness and not relying on the ground crew; even when using reliable headsets. In the future; we will be even more alert during pushback having seen how quickly a bad situation can develop.

column121: On day 0 I was put on the engine change crew to continue with the remove & replace of #2 engine on aircraft x. My first job was to apply the protective coating on the bottom of the aft engine mount due to corrosion that was found during the after removal of engine lower pylon inspection. Upon first application of the primer i noticed that the bottom outboard mating surface of the aft engine mount had in my opinion a substantial amount of pitting. I ceased operation and notified the inspector of my finding. The inspector did a visual of the area and told me that it was ok to continue the application of the second coat and the area was within limits.the initial found fault of corrosion found during the engine inspection was already documented and signed off as removed corrosion per the applicable aircraft maintenance manual (amm). I initially took his word for it and continued because i was just coming to a somewhat extensive and lengthy job and assumed that everything had been researched and performed per any applicable amm or structural repair manual (srm). While waiting on the paint to cure enough for work to be performed i did start research in the srm to look for limitations on corrosion in certain areas. I found a few items in the srm that went over engine mounts and brought it to the inspectors attention. There were some limits that we went over and came to agreement that .020 was a max allowable limit on certain areas. I do recall looking mainly in the srm i did also eventually look in the amm and found a ref for the inspection of the aft engine mount. At this point i was still taking into consideration that he is a quality control inspector and that he has  more extensive training in limits and expectations of repairs of damaged areas on the aircraft as well as the experience of seeing discrepancies like this on a more regular basis. After we had hung the engine and installed engine mount bolts i looked back at the task card and noticed that the engine install( the task the inspector said was used for the inspection) referenced the removal of corrosion amm for both the inspection of the lower pylon fwd and aft fittings as well as the lower longeron and the remove corrosion if found item. In my opinion i could not see how you can use a reference to remove corrosion as a reference for doing an inspection. I went to the amm for the inspection of the aft engine mount and found that it calls out for the removal of the mount itself to do the inspection. I then brought it up to everybody i believe and pressed the issue until we were instructed to remove the engine by our manager. We subsequently found a substantial amount of corrosion in the pylon bolt holes at the point where i went off shift. I was questioned as to why; if i believed that the pitting corrosion was not in limits then why would i assist in the engine install up to the point of where i called for the removal. The only answer i can give is that i was trusting of the judgement of my fellow mechanic/inspector but for my sake and the safety of the aircraft/lives i was still going to continue research until i was either satisfied with the inspectors signoff or i found documented evidence that disputed him. I was concerned about flight safety and my fellow union members that were working on it and was willing to call for the engine removal no matter what step of the install we were on. For the human factors i believe i can attribute: 1: lack of communication on my part by not communicating my concern to someone outside like technical support/engineering/maintenance control; 2 lack of knowledge: not knowing the corrosion limits and stopping the job until everybody was in agreement that the aircraft was safe in a timely manner; 3 lack of assertiveness: not injecting my concerns severity sooner.;  this report has been submitted in good faith and the events/timeline that happened have been reported to the best of my recollection.

column121: Event: Pilot A (Instructor) and Pilot B (member tasked to look after the plane 'MX OFFICER') took the C172S for a maintenance checkout flight after the 100hr inspection with Maintenance at ZZZ. The fuel tanks had no visible debris. The left tank had 15 gal and the right tank had 16 gal of 100LL. The right tank had tiny water droplets (about 1 mm); which were poured away. No water observed in the left tank. Three laps in the pattern (.6 of hobbs time) were completed without issue. The plane was placed back in service. No fuel was added given that there was a line at the fuel pumps and the fuel truck was not available. The next flight was scheduled right after the end of this flight. The next flight was an aircraft transition training flight with Pilot A (Instructor) and Pilot C (PPL only with about 240hrs). Three laps in the pattern were completed. The first lap was Go Around due to a gust during flare making the aircraft climb. Pilot C initiated a Go Around. The second lap was a normal landing and takeoff (touch and go). During the third lap; Pilot C completed a GUMPSS flow: fuel selector BOTH; mixture FULL RICH; light switches ON and seat and seat belts SECURED. Once abeam the numbers; Pilot C reduced the power and aimed for 1500 RPMs. The RPMs showed 1200 RPMs. Pilot C realized the difference and slightly added power. The MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) displayed 1700 RPMs. Pilot C was distracted by the RPM settings and started to extend the downwind leg while descending. Pilot A noticed a change in propeller sound different from the usual increase in RPMs and similar to an rudder only turn during cruise. Pilot A checked the position of the 'ball' in the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and confirmed it was centered. Pilot A then noticed the altitude of about 600' MSL and prompted a turn to base. Pilot C noticed higher than usual RPM changes and asked Pilot A to take over to rule out Pilot C's improper throttle changes. Pilot A took controls during the base turn and confirmed the propeller sound was still present and decided to do a full stop landing to troubleshoot on the ground. Pilot C agreed. Pilot A turned final and confirmed the fuel selector was BOTH; fuel shut off was IN; mixture was FULL RICH; and magnetos were on BOTH. Oil pressure was in the green arc; oil temperature was in the green arc and fuel flow was still in the green arc. When Pilot A confirmed the aircraft could glide to the runway; he reduced the throttle to IDLE. The propeller slowed down more than usual. Over the numbers; Pilot A set the flaps to 20 degrees (10 degrees already added on downwind). After touchdown the propeller stopped windmilling and came to a complete stop. Pilot A used the energy remaining to let the aircraft roll to the first exit; ([Taxiway] 1) and called [clear of the runway attempting to roll all the way clear]. After crossing the taxi intersection; Pilot A applied brakes and brought the aircraft to a complete stop. Pilot A called Pilot B and reported the issue. Pilot A restarted the plane without prime and the aircraft started without a problem. The aircraft was taxied to its parking spot and shutdown. A magneto ground check did not show any issues. Pilot B met the aircraft with a representative of Maintenance. The aircraft was secured and was not refueled. What I believed caused the problem:I believe the throttle control settings may caused the problem. After repeated use of the throttle controls the settings inside the cowling may have come loose and caused the engine to stop. I believe something was not properly secured during the 100hr inspection. No debris or water was found after inspection of the fuel sumps (left; right and engine). There were no changes in the mixture during flight. The aircraft restarted and taxied without problems on the ground. Not sure what can be done to prevent the recurrence

column121: We were enroute to MWC.  We were eventually cleared direct to MWC.  We were in between layers at 6000 ft with an overcast deck about 2000 ft below.  Handed off to MKE approach.  We rejected a descent to lower stating that we wanted to stay above the deck as long as possible to avoid any potential icing.  ATC cleared us direct IVALY; cross at or above 2600 ft; cleared the RNAV 4L approach to MWC; circle to runway 33R.  We descended to 4500 ft just above the deck; crossed IVALY and began an expedited descent to the next step down of 2300 ft at OWYAL.  We broke out at about 3000 ft  and advised approach with a report of light rime ice at about 3500 and our break out altitude just above 3000. Approach instructed us to contact tower.  At this point we were still about 3 miles from OWYAL.  We contacted tower with position reported as outside OWYAL.  Tower asked if we wanted to land runway 4L or circle to 33R; winds 300 at 10kts.  We elected to circle and tower said 'circle southwest of the airport and enter left base for 33R.'  We had the airport in sight and began to maneuver to enter an extended left base for 33R descending to  pattern altitude of 1745 ft.  Tower calls out an altitude alert saying 'we don't have a standard approach altitude.'  We believe we were cleared on a visual segment of the approach via circling instructions.  We replied that we were entering an extended left base for 33R and asked tower to confirm that we were cleared to land.  Cleared to land 33R ahead of traffic from the NE.  Landed and cleared at taxiway C; B; B1 with no further comment or issue.  Why the altitude alert?  Tower may have been tracking the profile for a straight in approach to 4L which would have alerted the altitude below the stepdown floor of 2300 prior to reaching OWYAL.  Raises another question:  when should you break off your approach and begin circling?  Wait until the MAP?  Or proceed visual when cleared to circle while maintaining visual contact with the airport?    Wait until within the circling radius for your category?  At the MDA the protected area at the circling altitude for category A aircraft is 1.1 nm radius from the approach end of the runway.  But at pattern altitude the whole class D area should be OK.

column121: While flying day; VMC to DEN RWY34R; we were cleared for the visual approach on a dogleg heading and 9000' with instructions to maintain 170 kts to CORDE (FAF). FO had a 2 mile ring around CORDE for SA; and as a spot where he briefed he would drop the gear and call for flaps 15. FO armed the approach but we did not set a lower altitude. CORDE altitude is 7000' or above. Just outside of the 2 mile ring from the FAF I mentioned that we were high and needed a lower altitude set with the autopilot on; did he want 7000?  We then set 7000' and the plane began a shallow descent; but we were still high. Just inside the 2 mile ring (1.5 miles from CORDE) we were 600-700' high and going higher on the path. We lowered the gear; he called for flaps 15; and began to slow to his target speed of 160. We were now over 800' high; and I mentioned that it would be helpful to keep his speed up to lose the required altitude. He responded by increasing the MCP speed back toward 170 with the autopilot on. When I saw that we were over 1000' high on the path deviation scale I told him we that wasn't going to do it; we needed to get the nose down and increase our rate of descent; whereupon he disengaged the autopilot and pitched down a bit. We also went flaps 25 at this point. I assessed that we were too high to use V/S to capture glideslope from above in time to make the stabilization windows; but we were nearing glideslope as he hand flew the plane; at between 165-170 kts. I told him that the 1000' window was coming up; we should reduce the descent rate from what I recall was reading over 1800 fpm.Big failure on my part was that; as I was distracted with helping correct the descent rate and glideslope; I failed to mention that we still did not have final flaps at the 1000' window.FO was able to arrest the rate of descent; but; as we were nearing 600'; I recall that the PAPI was displaying 4 red (low); and we got a couple of 'glideslope' calls. As we were still slowing to our target speed I felt that by leveling off he would recapture glideslope from below about the same time we would hit our target speed; so I figured we'd be able to achieve the 500' stability window. However; as we neared the 500' window we received a 'too low; terrain' call and went around. The 'too low; terrain' call surprised me; as we were completely VMC and nowhere near dangerous terrain on final; but I then realized that we were not at flaps 30. I know that will sometimes cause a 'too low; terrain' call instead of a 'too low; flaps' call; which would've been more obvious as to what was wrong.In hindsight a 'too low; terrain' callout should be followed by a terrain escape maneuver instead of the go-around that we did.The go-around was uneventful; as was the subsequent landing on RWY35R.

column121: On Day 0; I was pilot flying ZZZ1-ZZZ. When descending on the ZZZZZ arrival between 10;000-11;000 MS; we got an EICAS message of HYD 2 LO PRESSURE. I looked on the hydraulics page and there was no hydraulic pressure in system 2. The Captain requested ATC assistance and advised approach that we had XX souls on board and 4900 pounds of fuel. The Captain requested vectors so that we could stay out of the way of other aircraft and could run the checklist per the QRH. Once the Captain located the checklist he started going through it and while doing it; we also got the SPOILER FAULT EICAS message. The Captain completed the HYD 2 LO PRESSURE checklist items and HYD 2 LO PRESSURE remained annunciated; after that he worked on the SPOILER FAULT checklist and once that was completed; SPOILER FAULT extinguished. The Captain then calculated the landing numbers to get the appropriate V-speeds and landing distance. Once he got those numbers we transferred controls and he became the flying pilot and I became pilot monitoring.When the Captain called for gear down I moved the gear selector and the gear did not come down and we got the LG LEVER DISAGREE EICAS message. After completing this checklist; it called to go to the Alternate Landing Gear Extension Checklist which we completed and the gear came down.  After this; we notified ATC that we were ready to come in for landing; they gave us runway XX L which is up sloping. This was the most ideal choice as it would aid in stopping the aircraft. The landing was successful and soft but the plane did not have nose wheel steering; so differential braking was used to keep directional control. The Captain was able to slow the aircraft enough to make the high speed exit and clear the runway and make a slight right turn onto taxiway 1. Once on taxiway 1; the aircraft was stopped and we notified tower that we would need to stay there until we could get tugged in.Once tower was notified; the Captain notified the passengers; operations; and dispatch of the issue. We left the plane in the landing configuration; started the APU and left both engines running until the tug arrived. After waiting 25-30 minutes; tug came and we secured both engines and got towed. Once at the gate; all passengers deplaned and the Captain spoke to the dispatch supervisor and Maintenance Control and made the appropriate logbook entries.Cause: Aircraft loss of Hydraulic System 2.Suggestions: As second in command; I could've done a better job suggesting that we get in contact with dispatch; the passengers; and the flight attendants to keep everyone informed on the situation.

column121: On Day 0; I; Captain A; was operating flight ABCD from ZZZ1 to ZZZ as Pilot Monitoring. While on the ZZZZZ X arrival into ZZZ; at around 10;000 to 11;000 MSL; HYD 2 LO PRESS appeared on the EICAS. I looked at the Hydraulics page on the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) and noticed that there was no hydraulic pressure within system 2. I requested priority handling with ZZZ Approach; notified the controller of the fuel on board; which I believe was roughly 4900 pounds of fuel at the time; and that there were XX souls on board the aircraft. Because I was not the only operational aircraft arriving at ZZZ at the time; I requested with the approach controller to be vectored off the arrival procedure to stay out of the way while I began working on the QRH checklist items. I located the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist within the QRH and began going through the listed items. While completing this checklist; SPOILER FAULT also appeared on the EICAS. I continued with the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist items and completed the checklist. Once completed; HYD 2 LO PRESS remained annunciated. I began working on the SPOILER FAULT checklist. After completing the checklist items; SPOILER FAULT extinguished from being displayed on the EICAS. Following this; I used the non-normal section of the ERJ landing app to set the appropriate Vspeeds for landing. At that point I took control of the aircraft as Pilot Flying from First Officer Person B and had him run the Loss of Hydraulic System 2 QRH checklist.Once the landing gear was extended and all checklist items were complete; ZZZ ATC was notified that we were ready to come in for a landing. The landing runway that we were using was XXL as it is an upsloping runway. It was decided that this would be the best course of action to aid in stopping the aircraft. Additionally; I had also requested that emergency services follow the aircraft up the runway after we land. The landing was successful and soft. Because I had no rudder control or nosewheel steering upon touchdown; differential braking was used to keep directional control of the aircraft. I was able to slow the aircraft enough to make a slight right turn onto Taxiway 1; clear the runway; and make another slight right turn onto Taxiway 2. At that point; I stopped the aircraft; communicated with the tower controller that I would need to remain in the current position; as I was unable to make larger right or left turns and would have to be towed into the gate.After communicating with the tower controller; I informed the passengers; operations; and dispatch of the issue; and that the airplane would have to be towed to the gate. I left the aircraft in the landing configuration; started the APU; and left both engines running until the tug arrived roughly 25 to 30 minutes later. Once the tug arrived; I secured both engines; the tug was attached to the aircraft; and the aircraft was successfully towed to gate XX. Once at the gate; all passengers were deplaned; dispatch transferred me to a supervisor to notify them of the event; and I conversed with Maintenance Control in the logbook entry for the event.Cause: Aircraft loss of hydraulic system 2.Suggestions: According to the HYD 2 LO PRESS QRH checklist; if the HYD 2 LO PRESS remains annunciated on the EICAS; after turning the associated HYDRAULIC ELEC PUMP to the OFF position; the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist is complete; and I am supposed to complete the LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2 checklist. Instead of doing this; I went ahead and completed the SPOILER FAULT checklist instead. Had I continued with the LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2 checklist; as I should have; I would have known that it is stated not to accomplish the SPOILER FAULT checklist.Additionally; because of the feeling stress; I failed to inform the dispatcher; the flight attendants; and the passengers of the situation at hand. Looking back at the situation; I had plenty of time and fuel remaining that I could have accomplished communicating with dispatch; the flight attendants; and the passengers.

column121: In cruise; we noticed lightning on the horizon across a very wide area and activated the on-board radar. The tops were stratiform in all directions. The stratiform layer rose as we progressed; so we requested FL360 to maintain the ability to corroborate what we were seeing outside with the weather radar. The radar began painting a few isolated cells in the vicinity of ZZZZZ when we were 160nm away. The cells appeared well-defined and reasonably dispersed. We discussed a preliminary plan for diverting around the weather and agreed to proceed unchanged until we were approximately 80nm from the cells where we would have a more clearly-defined understanding of the weather as depicted on the radar. We also coordinated with center to verify the information we were seeing. At approx 80nm from ZZZZZ; we began a left deviation with the intention to later turn right direct the ZZZ VOR and then direct ZZZ. According to on board radar and center control; this was a safe path well clear of cells. As a matter of caution; I turned on the seatbelt sign and ordered the flight attendants to take their jump seats. We were still in smooth air; but conditions began to deteriorate to occasional and then to continuous moderate. The FO said to take over the airplane if I felt it necessary. Suddenly; airspeed dropped precipitously by approx 30kias. I said;Power! Power!" to the FO. He rapidly responded by applying TOGA power and asked if APR was necessary. I said no as airspeed was rapidly recovering. It is important to note the weather radar had previously showed no weather at or beneath the location where this happened at any point leading up to or at this location. Moments later; the autopilot disconnected as the airplane lurched suddenly into approximately 20 degrees of left bank and 7 degrees of pitch up accompanied by a rapid loss of airspeed. I took control of the airplane and called;"My aircraft." I leveled the nose immediately and leveled the wings while simultaneously reapplying TOGA thrust. Focused on maintaining attitude; I allowed deviations in altitude but remained very conscious of airspeed as it fell. I ordered the FO to call a descent to FL340 to ATC as a means of maintaining airspeed as the airspeed was initially completely unresponsive to the increased thrust and I felt a descent necessary to stay on the correct side of the power curve. In approximately negative 2 degrees of pitch; the airplane initially began descending to approx FL355 and then rapidly climbed to approx FL365 while still pitched down as the airspeed rapidly recovered before the FO could inform ATC. The airplane came back under positive control and I modified my instructions to the FO; 'Inform ATC of a severe turbulence encounter with deviations +/-500 feet.' The airplane remained under positive control thereafter; although for 5 or 10 minutes a very high thrust setting (CLB) was frequently necessary to maintain .75M; which we had been flying at before; during; and after the encounter. I returned control to the FO and the rest of the flight proceeded as normal except for a later STALL FAIL caution message in the descent to ZZZ. No one was injured and there was no apparent damage to the aircraft."
column123: In cruise at FL340 we notice build up from weather ahead; our radars indicated widespread perception in direction of our flight. After talking to ATC with the information they made available to us we requested to climb to FL360 and received the clearance to do. Looking at the on board radar and talking to center about what they're seeing up ahead; we determined it was best to deviate left of course where there weren't any radar echos on the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) or what ATC was seeing on their side. We request a deviation left of course and receive the approval. A few minutes into the new cruise altitude; we start getting moderate chop to moderate turbulence with airspeed fluctuations requiring me to put in TOGA thrust to get back up .75 Mach. When then hit severe turbulence getting major altitude and airspeed fluctuations disabling the autopilot. Captain took over pilot flying duties and I took over pilot monitoring duties during the upset recovery from the severe turbulence. We alerted/requested ATC that we were descending from FL360 to FL340; for a greater buffet boundary as we were having a hard time maintaining airspeed and altitude due to the turbulence. After leveling at FL340 the fluctuations continued with moderate chop to moderate turbulence. The turbulence stopped approximately 3 minutes after leveling at FL340; we determined with the radar and ATC that it was clear ahead. I called in the back to talk to the flight attendants to make sure everyone was okay and no one was hurt. The captain gave me control of the aircraft back and rest of the flight proceeded as normal; except for receiving a STALL FAIL caution message in the descent into ZZZ.

column123: The entire flight experienced quite a lot of turbulence enroute. None of us slept well and there we were all quite fatigued on the approach. I left VNAV and verbally announced FLCH to desend to the 1700 final approach fix after being cleared for the approach. The Captain Monitoring did not apparently did not hear or see I was in FLCH. The Captain believed we were still in VNAV and dialed the altitude down to touchdown elevation outside of the FAF. We descended below the glide path and when the Relief Pilot and I noticed it I disconnected the autopilot to climb back to the glide path. Our airspeed decayed to about 10 knots below Vref. No airspeed alert or shaker was activated. I quickly pushed the thrust up to regain the airspeed and glide path. The Tower gave us a momentary low altitude alert but we were fully stable by 500 feet and performed a normal landing.

column121: After closing the doors and pulling the jet bridge back; we made contact with the ramper crew who was just off the right side of our nose. I (Captain) asked for the phraseology to allow us to release brake. The ramper told us all secure below; FOD walk complete; steering disengaged; ready for brake release." I then released the parking brake and responded with "parking brake released; clear to capture; we are calling for the push now." The aircraft then began rolling backwards at an unusual rate. An operations manager in a truck off the right side of the nose then yelled and told us to set the brakes. Both the First Officer and I applied pressure to the toe brakes however they didn't actuate so I instead pulled the parking brake and we came to a stop.The cause is most likely due to lack of communication between flight crew and rampers; ramper's fatigue; and complacency. After making initial contact via headset; I believe the ramper just instinctively gave his whole prior to pushback brief without fully confirming everything he stated.Suggestions: I recommend rampers to be more thorough with their instructions; making sure that each topic they speak about is true by visually confirming it. As a pilot; we could also start using a double confirmation before changing configurations; such as releasing the brake of disconnecting inter-phones."
column123: Once jet bridge was pulled Captain called for rampers via operations since no one had answered our calls down below. Operations manager pulled up in a truck and spoke with the crew chief who then looked at us. I pointed to my headset and that established comms between the flight deck and ramp. Captain asked if they were ready for brake release for which the crew chief responded with all secure below FOD walk complete ready for brake release." At this point Captain disengaged the parking brake. The aircraft started to roll a little as it normally does but soon it rolled a lot more than usual. Operations manager yelled and we were already trying to stop the aircraft from moving. I used the toe brakes but due to no hydraulic pressure they were ineffective. Captain then engaged the parking brake to stop the aircraft. After that the crew chief walked back over to the aircraft and secured the airplane to the tug. Everything from there proceeded as normal however it took calling ramp twice to get them to push the airplane once cleared.Cause: Lack of proper communication and complacency by ramp crew. We released the parking brake when the ramp agent gave his brief and stated ready for brake release.Suggestions: I should've made sure that the ramp agent was actually focused on the act of pushing the aircraft. By waiting until he was done talking to the operations manager we could've prevented a situation in which the aircraft was in fact not secured to the tug."

column121: While enroute to ZZZ at approximately 4000 ft. and about 8 miles to the west of the airfield we're cleared for a visual approach to Runway XXL. We had the visual approach to XXL with a 5-mile final; loaded into the FMS for reference. I knew the airport elevation was 800 ft. so that would give us a pattern altitude of 2300 ft. From our position relative to the field we decided to enter the pattern on a left base for the runway. After being cleared for the visual approach I began a descent to pattern altitude. While descending and at approximately 2500 we heard the alert from the GPWS warning us of terrain. I was hand flying at the time so I immediately added power and arrested the descent and then initiated a climb. We climbed up to approximately 3000 ft and continued on a heading that coincided with a left base for XXL. As we approached final; maybe 1 mile prior; I again began a descent for pattern altitude. Once on final a higher than normal descent rate was needed to get on profile; but we were able to get back on profile well before our 500 ft. stabilized call out. The rest of the approach and landing were normal.Alerted by GPW System. Cause: Unfamiliar with terrain west of airport as this was my first ever approach and landing in this direction. Also; night time darkness. Immediate level off and climb to higher altitude. Suggestions: More awareness / respect for first time landing on this runway.

column121: I'm in the CE-700 Longitude fleet. I've now attempted the RNAV RNP Z for Runway XX into ZZZ twice. In both cases the vertical guidance failed. The first time I believe I was being vectored onto the final approach course around ZZZZZ; and the second time I was on the Radius-to-Fix (RF) leg just past ZZZZZ1. The position and altitude of the events were similar. In both cases I was where I should be; doing what I should have been doing; and the VNAV just gives up. It won't allow you to transition to a glide path (GP) (which is armed in the background); it just gives up on vertical guidance altogether while in VPATH.Suggestions: Given that it has been two different airframes on two different trips while at a similar position; I would say that a pattern is forming. We proceed to stop the climb out and stop at 7;000 feet to stop the cabin from climbing.Prior to departure we did write up that the N1 gauges were showing a big split between each other on the ground at the gate. Maintaience came and looked at the issue which was written up a similar way for this aircraft earlier. I questioned that choice and spoke with the dispatcher; duty pilot and Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control went through the previous write up and looked to see what was done. I was informed that the problem the aircraft had for the pressurization issue prior was not related with the pack and that they performed tests of pressurization in accordance with Boeing standard procedures. After speaking with Maintenance Control my FO and I were comfortable taking the aircraft as they said what test and checks were done by maintenance and the plane was safe to continue for service.Once we leveled off and communicated with ATC. I immediately directed my attention to the abnormal indication and the FO and I accomplished the applicable QRH procedure for pressurization malfunction. The aircraft was leveled off as required and we began coordinating a return to ZZZ.Given the proximity to the departure airport; ATC coordination; aircraft configuration considerations; and time compression associated with the abnormal condition; my focus was primarily on safely flying the aircraft; completing the QRH; and setting up for the return and landing. The decision was made to return to ZZZ.During this period of high workload and compressed timeline; I overlooked referring the FOM for additional considerations related to overweight landing and did not formally declare an emergency with ATC. ATC was informed about what the situation was and that we were doing a checklist and our plans to return to ZZZ. The QRH checklist was followed for the overweight landing and what to expect and to do a landing assessment. In that QRH under additional items which was after checklist completion it had a few lengthy paragraphs about overweight landing characteristics and a line about going to the FOM for more guidance which I overlooked about the FOM. In retrospect; referencing the FOM would have prompted a formal emergency declaration due to the overweight landing condition.The approach and landing were uneventful. The aircraft landed safely without injury to passengers or crew and without aircraft damage. After clearing the runway; we coordinated with maintenance and completed the appropriate write-ups in the aircraft logbook regarding the pressurization malfunction and overweight landing.Upon reflection; this event reinforced the importance of deliberate consideration of administrative and procedural follow-through such as emergency declaration requirements even when the operational outcome appears controlled and manageable. In the future; I will ensure that; workload permitting; I take a moment to cross-check FOM guidance when abnormal situations involve potential overweight landings or other criteria requiring formal declaration.Safety was maintained throughout the event; and all required documentation was completed.Cause: Aircraft had recent pressurization-related write-up. The Right pack was re-MEL'd after being cleared.Although maintenance stated issue was unrelated; prior history may have increased system vulnerability. There is also a potential normalization of repeat discrepancy.I think to mitigate this would be to not dispatch an aircraft with a repeat item in the same day with similar write up issues and investigate the problem closer.
column123: While completing fms preflight tasks; I noticed that the takeoff N1 settings were mismatched and fluctuating. This mirrored a similar maintenance issue the previous crew had with this aircraft; that resulted in a loss of pressurization. Maintenance was already at the aircraft due to other write ups; and they were notified right away. Eventually; an MEL was applied to the right pack; but as the captain and I were noticing that this event felt very similar to the events leading up to the previous loss of pressurization; the captain called both the duty pilot and Maintenance Control to express our concern. Ultimately we felt convinced that the aircraft would be safe after a thorough explanation from Maintenance Control; explaining that a leak test was conducted; and that the right pack MEL and N1 differential was most likely not associated with the cause of the pressurization issue earlier in the day. After an hour from when maintenance was first called we pushed back. On departure we noted that the actual takeoff N1 settings were not within .5 percent of the performance data setting; but we interpreted that to be in accordance with the pack inoperative MEL. The taxi and take off went normally; but on the initial climb out we noticed cabin altitude climbing at around 2000 feet per minute; and our ears were popping. We leveled off at 7000; and the captain transferred radios to me(I was already pilot flying); and then notified dispatch. The bleeds were set in accordance with the MEL; with the right pack off; the left pack on; and the isolation valve closed. It was then determined that we should return to ZZZ; which was coordinated with dispatch and then ATC. The captain ran the overweight landing checklist; and the non routine landing considerations checklist; while I flew the aircraft and set up the aircraft for a landing in ZZZ. The cabin altitude warning checklist was not completed; as we never received a cabin altitude warning. Unfortunately both the captain and I missed that an emergency needed to be declared when landing overweight. We landed safely; and returned to gate XX; and all passengers were deplaned right away.Cause: I believe that a more thorough investigation by maintenance could have prevented this incident. Both myself and the captain continuously expressed concern about the similarities of our situation and the event described to us by the previous crew. With hindsight I wish we would've held more firm in not accepting the aircraft.

column121: This report is documenting a flight did not operate event for an airplane without an APU that we were scheduled to fly for two legs (ZZZ-ZZZZ-ZZZ1). The day before this; I operated Flight ABCD from ZZZZ1 to ZZZ without an APU. Although the APU was listed as inop in the MEL. ZZZ ops was not aware of the APU inop on arrival. Although we called ops on the ground in ZZZ to ensure power and air would be available at the gate (XX); they failed to have a jetway driver at the gate (so no ground power) and ground personnel were unaware that we would be leaving an engine running for en extended period of time; leading to an unsafe situation with the wing walker moving towards an operating engine and no control of vehicle traffic behind the aircraft.Report narrative of flight did not operate.Just prior to closing the aircraft door for departure out of ZZZ; the APU automatically shutdown. Maintenance accomplished a restart and the APU automatically shutdown a second time for high APU oil temperature. Maintenance informed me of their intentions to MEL the APU as inoperative for our next 2 legs through ZZZZ to ZZZ1. The temperature in ZZZZ was forecast to be 84 degrees; and I felt that would have caused uncomfortable cabin temperatures at the gate and on departure. In addition; my experience with issues of not having a gate agent/jetway driver upon arrival (for ground power from the jetway) as well as potential of having inexperienced ground personnel around a running engine; and language issues complicating communication; had me concerned about safety issues on arrival at these locations. For those reasons; I placed a flight did not operate entry in the logbook. Report narrative of Flight ABCD Day 0.Prior to boarding in ZZZZ1 with no ground power or conditioned air available at gate XY; the APU automatically shutdown. We accomplished the APU fault checklist and coordinated for maintenance; ground power; conditioned air for the cabin and for the potential need for pneumatic air cart. With coordination from maintenance and Maintenance Control we conducted an APU restart and the APU again automatically shutdown. The APU was MEL'd and we proceeded with appropriate supplemental procedures and coordination for departure. The weather in ZZZZ1 was 84 degrees and cloudy. We had conditioned air prior to boarding and all necessary ground equipment standing by. At the time; I felt ZZZ should be a competent station to safely receive an aircraft without an APU. The cabin temperature got uncomfortably warm during the crossbleed start but cooled relatively quickly in flight. The APU was in the MEL and we felt ZZZ should have been aware of the aircraft status for arrival. After an uneventful flight and landing on Runway XX in ZZZ; we called ZZZ ops on the short taxi to gate XX. The FO asked ops if power and electrics would be available immediately on arrival at [gate] XX. Ops said something like 'understand you are asking for power and air; does that mean you have an issue with your APU?' The FO responded that the APU was inop and we would need electrics and air conditioning at arrival. Ops told us power and air would be available but I don't recall their exact words.We taxied to the gate and set brakes. I looked towards the operating engine and saw the wing walker walking from the wing tip towards the operating engine. She took about four steps then stopped briefly before taking another step or two towards the running engine. I opened my window and motioned for her or someone on the ground to get her away from the left engine. I was prepared to shut the engine down if she continued moving towards it. A supervisor yelled in her direction and she moved outboard of and aft of the wing to stop traffic on the road behind us.I then looked at the jetway and realized we didn't have a jetway driver; and therefore had no ground power available. The FO called ops and asked for a jetway driver. The response was that an agent was on the way. The agent arrived at the gate a few minutes later and we waited for the jetway to be positioned before ground power could be provided to the plane.I felt the entire process of receiving an aircraft without an APU was handled without urgency or an understanding from ops or ground personnel of the potential dangers involved. I felt like we were communicating the situation but we weren't understood. To make matters worse; we had an FAA representative on the jump seat witnessing the entire event.

column121: We took off XXC in ZZZ. It was a flaps 5 bleeds on NADP (Noise Abatement Departure Procedure) 1 DEP. After calling flaps up after takeoff checklist; my FO noticed during the checklist that we had a R DUCT pressure of 80 psi and that the L DUCT pressure was only at 40psi. We then told ATC that we wanted to level off. They gave us 15000ft to do so. At that time I transferred the controls over to my FO as well as the radios and I started to focus on the issue. I remembered from previous flights that there is no real guidance on this issue other than a brief paragraph in the limitations section from the FM. Which states '  A duct pressure difference of more than 8 PSI may indicate a mechanicalmalfunction. If a duct pressure split is observed after bleeds are configured forflight; and the lowest indication is approximately 18 PSI or less; contactMaintenance. ' we had exceeded those numbers. when we leveled off at 15000 the duct pressure equaled out and seemed stabilized; but not having more info I had dispatch call us to get Maintenance Control on the radio. Maintenance Control did not have more guidance for us after verifying where gauges were saying at this time. They said that it would be ok to continue.  FO and I talked and agreed to try. We got clearance immediately to climb to FL230. Once power was added to initiate climb; the duct pressure needles again split with R DUCT going all the way to 80psi. Maintenance Control was still on the radio and we told them what happened. At that moment we decided to head back to ZZZ. Knowing that we were going to be very overweight we requested priority handling and had personnel waiting for us. We briefed each other; the FAs and passengers of the situation. We got the airplane ready for landing in ZZZ and landed without any incident. We exited the runway and had personnel verify our brake temps before entering the terminal area. Everything was normal and proceeded to the gate.

Weather at destination had been a bit variable over the time period we had been watching it prior to our arrival.340 to 360 5-8kts visibility was reporting 6-7 miles ceilings were 600+ temp just above freezing around 2-3c. Due to the high tail wind and decreasing weather conditions we were concerned with being able to land XX in ZZZ. Weather in ZZZ1 had been similar however wind had been reporting higher. There was a lot of discussion about the pros and cons of shooting the ILS to XX and landing with a tail wind vs LOC XX circle XY. We did run our EFB for both directions and they both worked with current conditions. However with the wind just below the limit at ZZZ1 made Captain nervous with conditions worsening. He called tower directly over the radio and got a weather report. I don't remember what that report was I believe higher winds from the north. He also mentioned tower hadn't had any traffic in a while so no runway condition report. Visibility was reporting plenty good so we opted for the LOC XX circle XY. On the approach we broke out higher than I was expecting however visibility was not what was reported. In particular on the south end of the field. We circled at the published MDA however we forgot about the NOTAM with a MDA 60ft higher. At the time we were both completely unaware we had made the mistake. Around the downwind to base leg tower gave us a low level alert which we confirmed our altitude. Shortly after we lost sight of the airport and went missed. Which leads to the second error. The turn away from the airport. Captain said I lost sight of the airport tell them we are going missed. I call tower and let them know; they acknowledged and told us to fly the published missed. Captian hits the go around button brings power up then makes no call outs. I query him about setting flaps to setting two. He replied flaps two. Then immediately calls gear up. I raised flaps to two and put the gear up. In the time period he started making a right turn away from the airport. I could tell he was behind the plane. I didn't want to cause more confusion or debate with correcting him at this point. So checked the chart for obstacles. When my eyes get back to the PFD (Primary Flight Display) I notice we are well beyond 30 degrees of bank so I called out bank angle. He corrects however is a little aggressive with the controls when he does. At this point we continue on with the missed and divert to ZZZ1.

column121: During pre-departure preparations for Flight ABCD (ZZZ-ZZZ1); maintenance personnel entered the flight deck approximately ten minutes before door closure to check oil levels and advised us they would service the No. 2 engine. We acknowledged and continued normal duties. After receiving matching passenger counts from the flight attendant and release; I authorized door closure. Both packs were operating at that time; and no abnormal odors were present.Seconds after the door closed; while awaiting the flight attendant's cabin secure" report; I detected an acrid; "old socks/burning" odor on the flight deck with no visible smoke. I immediately turned both packs off and opened the DV (direct vision) windows to ventilate. The flight attendant confirmed the odor was also present in the cabin. With windows open and recirculation fans on; the smell began to dissipate. I contacted Maintenance Control and described the situation. They requested that we turn each pack on individually to isolate the source. I expressed concern about reintroducing fumes; but they advised the effect should be minimal with ventilation.We briefed the flight attendant and instructed her to open the service door if the odor returned. Pack 1 produced no abnormal smell. Upon selecting Pack 2 on; the same strong acrid odor immediately returned; prompting us to turn Pack 2 off. The flight attendant opened the service door due to the intensity of the smell. At this point; I determined the aircraft was no longer safe for passengers or crew. I instructed the First Officer to contact Operations and request the jet bridge be reconnected for deplaning. I informed Maintenance Control that I was refusing the aircraft and contacted Dispatch to advise that a new aircraft would be required.After all passengers deplaned; the crew elected to seek medical evaluation out of caution. Vitals and blood samples were taken; no abnormalities were found. I experienced a scratchy throat; and medical staff advised it should resolve within 24 hours.Cause: I believe somehow the oil vapors or oil drippings got into the APU bleed system when they were servicing the engine number 2.Suggestions: Use O2 mask whenever it is needed. I didn't use it because I thought the ventilation with the windows open was enough. I ended up with a scratchy throat."

Once across runway XXL heading North on taxiway 1 I applied brakes to hold short of runway XXC. The aircraft brakes could not stop the jet like I was accustomed to. One; the aircraft had approximately 20K lbs more fuel than normal. Two; due to the weight of the aircraft; it's performance both on accelerating and braking was not what I have experienced in the past. Three; I was following direction to 'expedite'.Suggestions: In the future; I will tell ATC I'm unable to expedite if an aircraft is too heavy.

column121: While operating a 2020 Cessna 182T (G1000 NXi); under VFR with Flight Following; I experienced an in-flight electrical smoke event.En route with one practice landing at ZZZ1. After departing ZZZ1; I was established in cruise at 6;500 feet MSL in clear VMC conditions. I had completed the cruise checklist shortly before the event; and all indications were normal at that time.While in cruise; I observed a light puff of white smoke emanating from the left side of the instrument panel accompanied by a strong electrical odor. No visible flame was observed. At approximately the same time; the Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) went blank; the Primary Flight Display (PFD) and radio panel flickered intermittently; and the secondary radio became inoperative. No circuit breakers were found popped.I immediately requested priority handling with ZZZ [TRACON] and diverted to the nearest suitable airport; ZZZ. I pulled the MFD circuit breaker. The master and alternator were left on in order to retain primary radio communications during the diversion. No windows were opened; and no oxygen was used. The aircraft landed approximately 5-10 minutes after onset without further incident. There were no injuries.After landing; the avionics switches were observed to be heat-deformed/melted. No additional smoke was observed after the initial puff.Post-flight maintenance inspection reported no evidence of active fire. A malfunctioning avionics switch on BUS 2 was identified and replaced. Wiring behind the panel was inspected by maintenance personnel; and an independent avionics shop conducted an additional inspection prior to return to service.This report is submitted in the interest of safety documentation and analysis of an electrical smoke event involving heat deformation of panel components and partial avionics failure in flight.The problem arose in cruise flight at 6;500 feet MSL; shortly after completing the cruise checklist with normal indications; a light puff of white smoke was observed from the left side of the instrument panel accompanied by a strong electrical odor. Avionics degradation followed immediately.The event was first identified visually (smoke) and by smell (electrical odor); followed by loss of the MFD and intermittent operation of other avionics.The precise initiating failure is undetermined from the pilot's perspective. Post-flight maintenance identified a malfunctioning avionics switch on BUS 2. The relationship between that component and the in-flight smoke event was not independently determined by the reporting pilot.The presence of smoke in the cockpit was assessed as a potentially time-critical situation. Immediate priorities were aircraft control; communication; and expeditious landing. Priority handling was requested promptly. A decision was made to pull the MFD circuit breaker while leaving the master and alternator on in order to retain primary radio communication capability during the diversion.The event occurred unexpectedly during routine cruise flight. The presence of smoke created a heightened workload environment requiring rapid prioritization of tasks. Maintaining situational awareness and communication while managing a partial avionics degradation required focused attention.The aircraft was diverted to the nearest suitable airport (ZZZ) and landed within approximately 5-10 minutes of onset. The MFD circuit breaker was pulled. Other electrical components were not de-energized in order to preserve communication capability during the emergency descent and landing.The aircraft was removed from service pending maintenance evaluation. Maintenance reported no evidence of active fire. A faulty avionics switch on BUS 2 was replaced; wiring was inspected; and an independent avionics inspection was conducted prior to return to service.

The roll was estimated to be between 35-45 degrees. The Captain (PF) and myself (PM) both said; 'Upset' which the CPT (Captain) performed incredibly well. The aircraft initially did not roll to the left; in fact I still remember hearing the CPT slam the flight controls against the stop to the left as he tried to correct the a/c and the a/c did not respond. After recovery the CPT checked on the flight attendant and passengers and we continued with the approach. I notified ATC multiple times which until I informed them about how far we rolled (approx 35-45 degrees) and our actions to get back on the approach; they seemed to not understand the severity of the situation. Once clear of the runway the CPT made an announcement to the passengers for some reassurance. We continued to the gate without further issue.Cause is unknown.Contributing factors have to be the spacing of the 777 then the Airbus 320/321 a/c (Aircraft); however we did note that there was 5 mile spacing between the aircraft as shown on our map rings.Suggestions: Unsure; unless they would like to provide more spacing for regional jets following heavy a/c or 320/321 a/c on approach.

column123: After joining the ILS 28C approach course; we were made aware by ATC that there was a heavy Boeing 777 two spots in front of us; approximately 10nm ahead. Around 5 miles ahead of us was an Airbus 319/20. I think they both joined the final approach course around KOENN at 7;000 ft; making a right base-to-final turn from the North. We joined the approach from a Southeast arrival ( I believe it was the WATSN 4); so we joined a 30 nm straight in for the approach. It had been an uneventful flight; and good weather conditions with a small layer over the field but we were in VMC. The spacing seemed normal; so both me and my first officer weren't thinking wake turbulence would be an issue; however; around KOENN we got hit with significant wake turbulence. at first; the aircraft banked left about 10-20 degrees slowly; which we acknowledged as wake and the autopilot corrected promptly. As it was correcting back to straight-and-level; the aircraft sharply banked right between 40-50 degrees uncommanded . Both me and my first officer called 'Upset' simultaneously; and I hand flew the upset recovery procedure. I believe we lost around 400 feet of altitude in the recovery before I was able to get the wings level and the aircraft stabilized. My airspeed increased to around 220 knots before I slowed back to our assigned speed. While I was recovering; my First Officer made a call to ATC to let them know we were deviating and recovering; but stepped on someone else's transmission so ATC was unaware for about 2-3 minutes until we found space to talk to them and inform them of our situation. I returned to normal flight at 7000 ft. and once I had the autopilot back on I asked my first officer to reach out to the flight attendant to verify that everyone in the back was okay. My flight attendant said everyone was fine and no injuries; but that people were pretty nervous. We reported no injuries to ATC when they asked. Since I was around 15 miles away from landing I decided to continue approach to land; which was uneventful. After clearing the runway; I set the parking brake and made a passenger announcement to apologize for the bumpy ride; and explained to them that it was due to wake turbulence from an aircraft in front of us. We then went to the gate; deplaned; and I called the Manager and filled out a report. Then we continued our flight day.Wake turbulence induced the undesired aircraft state. Busy radios made communicating with ATC during the upset recovery messy.Suggestions: I think this was an unavoidable event. Spacing and altitude seemed good to me; and we did a textbook upset recovery procedure prescribed by Standard Operating Procedures.

column121: In Month 2; while I was off duty; my peer ZZZ QC (Quality Control) Inspector Person A completed a borescope re-inspection on Aircraft X #1 engine; S/N XXXXXX. She determined that the previously deferred (Logbook Deferral Sheet XXXXXXX) burn holes had grown axially but remained on the same 150-hour re-inspection interval.Two days later; Maintenance Control Technician Person B forwarded an email to the List of the ZZZ QC shop. The email was between Person C a powerplant engineer and Person D; an engineer. The Email explained they did not agree with the axial measurements and the worst radial measurements appeared to be 0.177 inch and per the AMM (72-XX-XX-XXX-XXX-XXX-X) the item should be on a 750-hour re-inspection interval.Upon my return to work; I read the email and checked the online system to find that Maintenance Person B had changed the re-inspection interval to the 750-hour limit from the 150-hour re-inspection interval applied in ZZZ1 on Month 1due to power plant engineer Person E conferring with Person D. It is my understanding that Maintenance Control is not to change inspection department findings without an approved document. A review of the facts found that ZZZ2 had originally placed this deferral on a 300-hour re-inspection. However; under ZZZ2; deferral reference; dated Month 0; identified a 150 hour re-inspect but a 750-hour re-inspection per the engineer.In Month 1; ZZZ1 Inspector Person F dropped the original limit from its initial 300-hour re-inspection to a 150-hour inspection. Following this change; ZZZ2; ZZZ1 and ZZZ QC Inspectors completing re-inspections all determined the limit should remain on a 150-hour inspection interval The AMM (72-XX-XX-XXX-XXX-XXX-Y) states Accept with an inspection each 750 hours if The LE hole beyond the 50 percent span is less than 0.10 in. (2.54 mm) axially and less than 0.20 in. (5.08 mm) radially.There are multiple pictures on the QC Borescope file showing that the radial holes are larger than 0.20 in. To me; this would be either a 30- hour re-inspection or a 150- hour re-inspection depending on how the axial dimensions are measured. We have a measurement training guide that shows the way all of our inspectors measured it; we also have the email from Person D stating to measure from where the nose of the leading-edge airfoil would have been back the end of the damage. I emailed Maintenance to have the deferral revised. However; to date; I have not received a response except from our supervisor Person G who suggested he will investigate this matter. but is currently training at another station.Cause: Maintenance changed a re-inspection interval without advising the staff involved with the limit; without having supporting Technical Data.Suggestions: Prohibit having Maintenance changing discrepancies and limits entered by others.

column121: I and a low hour student pilot were conducting a night training flight at ZZZ.  Winds were 230 at 6 and we chose to use runway XX for departure.  We left the ramp making a call on CTAF that we would be back taxiing on RWY XY.  While on taxi; I observed an aircraft inbound from the north and asked my student to locate it. While on the taxiway between the two runways we watched as the aircraft approached and passed to the west of the airfield.  I could see it was an air ambulance helicopter and believed they were going to land at their hanger.  We called out our back-taxi on CTAF on RWY XX and proceeded down the runway to the run-up pad and conducted a standard run-up and pre-takeoff brief.  We lined up on XX and announced our departure on CTAF.Off the departure end of RWY XX at about 700 ft AGL; my student suddenly yelled 'TRAFFIC!!' and made abrupt control inputs; climbing and banking left.  Before I had a chance to react; I saw the helicopter pass in front and below us through the lower right corner of the windscreen; and then out my side window maybe 50-100 feet below.  We regained our composure and the student decided to continue with the flight.I would later ask the student when and where the helicopter was when he first saw it. He stated it was at about his ten o'clock and close enough to see the pilots face if it had been daylight.Back in the office; I asked the line staff if they heard our radio calls and if he heard or saw the helicopter. He stated the helicopter came in and set down at their hanger; shut down for about thirty seconds; started back up and immediately took off. He said he heard our departure call on RWY XX as the helicopter left the ground and started flying north through the two rows of hangers and passed by the office at high speed and rooftop level.  He said he has never heard a helicopter take off that loud before.  He thought to himself that the helicopter was going to fly right through (our) departure path.  He said at no time did he hear them on CTAF.This near mid-air collision could have been avoided had the helicopter pilot been at least monitoring CTAF and heard our departure call.
