column121: On Day 0; I departed ZZZ to ZZZ1 for the purpose of practicing tower operations at an unfamiliar airport. After two landings at ZZZ1 with a couple hours of leisure flight in between the landings; I departed ZZZ1 for my return to ZZZ. My eta at ZZZ was approximately XA:00; and; based on the weather data available through my EFB; my expectation was an arrival on RWY XX at ZZZ. The flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ was unremarkable in all regards. Approximately 10 miles east of ZZZ; I obtained the weather via the ZZZ AWOS system; which indicated winds from 020 at 9 kts. As expected; the winds favored an arrival on RWY XX; so I set up for a slightly wider than normal righthand base entry for RWY XX. There was no local traffic in the pattern; and the only radio traffic was from a single inbound plane approximately 10 miles out for RWY XX.I descended to pattern altitude at approximately 5 miles from ZZZ; added 10 degrees of flaps; and entered the right base for RWY XX pitched to approximately 90 kts. Upon turning north for final; approximately 2-3 miles south of ZZZ; I noted the winds aloft at pattern altitude seemed brisker than the AWOS report and I felt slight gusting; which was consistent with my prior experience at altitude and generally unremarkable. Because of the ground level crosswind and the gusting at pattern altitude; I decided to make my landing with 20 degrees flaps; rather than my normal 30 degrees; and adjust my final approach speed up from my normal 65-70 kts to something in the low to mid 70 kts range.During final approach; I added the second 10 degrees of flaps approximately one mile from the threshold and I maintained a crab angle into the wind; which meant my heading was east of the runway heading; as expected. I adjusted my pitch after adding the second notch of flaps and was holding a pretty steady 72 kts airspeed with 20 degrees of flaps. Upon reaching short final; I added left rudder to transition from a crab heading to runway heading using a 'right wing low slip technique' and continued to hold approximately 72 kts. The slight gusting I had experienced at pattern altitude was no longer evident at short final altitude. Overall; the final approach felt stable and my airspeed and heading varied very little from the initial turn final until the threshold; except for the intentional airspeed adjustment associated with adding the second notch of flaps.As I crossed the threshold; I pulled power to idle; compensated for the slight nose down action associated with the 182 when power is brought to idle; and entered the ground effect. Flight in the ground effect was stable; and my runway placement was slightly left of center but certainly within the middle third of the runway.When my airspeed dissipated sufficiently; I began my flare for touchdown. At this point; I experienced a gust (presumably) that caused the plane to yaw noticeably and abruptly to the left; which resulted in me being in a 'right wing low' bank with the right main leading the left main. I was expecting to touchdown any moment; so my reaction was to correct the left yaw by adding right aileron to bring the nose to the right and toward the center of the runway. In doing so; I believe I overcorrected for the left yaw and ended up pointing too far to the right when I touched down; which occurred immediately after making my correction.The touchdown led with the right main; which would have been oriented farthest to the south at this point due to the overcorrection. After the right main touched down; the left main and nose gear followed; either at the same time or perhaps with the left main slightly ahead of the nose. The touchdown itself was not particularly hard; although I wouldn't hold it out as my smoothest landing by any means.At this point; elapsed time became a little difficult to judge; but it seems like within a second or two after touchdown; I felt a force acting on the plane that I hadn't experienced before; and that caused me to pause for another second or two in order to evaluate what I was experiencing. I determined the force was sideloading toward my left; and I also noticed the left wing of the plane was dipping and the right main had come off the runway; resulting in the plane rolling only on the left main and the nose gear. I responded to the side loading by adding what little remaining right aileron I had left and pressing the left rudder pedal aggressively. Unfortunately; neither control input seemed to help; and I believe the sideloading actually caused the nose wheel to turn to the right because the plane began rolling across the runway in a right arc. The tilt to the left gradually increased to the point where I actually leaned to the passenger side of the plane in an attempt to offset it. At some point; I heard a rubbing noise I didn't recognize; and my first reaction was to look out the left window to see if the left wingtip was dragging the ground. It did not seem to be close to dragging; so I assumed the rubbing noise was coming from the nose gear being in a bind or something along those lines (I later learned the noise was the prop contacting the runway surface).After arcing to the right across the runway for a couple seconds (which felt like an hour) with all the right aileron and left rudder I had to provide; the plane leaned back to the right and settled on all three gears. At this point; I engaged the brakes pretty aggressively and came to a stop about three feet from the right edge of RWY XX with the engine running smoothly at idle. I'm guessing at this point; but it seems the nose of the plane was pointing about 040 or 050 at the time. Suffice it to say; the rightward arc I traveled across the runway was significant in any event.I looked out the windows of the plane and noted a runway light less than a wing width away toward my left; and; based on my proximity to the runway edge; I didn't think I had enough room to attempt a left turn on the runway without risking an impact with the runway light. As a result; I elected to exit the runway to the east; make a lefthand arc through the RSA; and reenter the runway between the next set of runway lights; so that's how I proceeded. The exit and reentry of the runway was smooth and uneventful; so I proceeded north down RWY XX to the next taxiway intersection and exited the runway. While taxiing down the runway; I heard the plane behind me call a five-mile final; so I announced myself upon exiting the runway and noted the traffic was on short final at that point.I taxied uneventfully back to the hangar and shut down the engine; and when the propeller came to a stop; I realized the tips were all curled; hence the unexplained noise I heard while arcing across the runway. This was the first time I realized a prop strike had occurred.At the time of the occurrence; I held a private pilot license with an instrument rating; as well as high performance and complex endorsements. I had 314.9 hours of total time; with 287.2 as PIC. Specific to C182 time; I had a total of 81.0 hours and 100 landings; 40 of which were night landings. In the last 180 days; I had 20.8 hours in a C182 and 18 landings; 7 of which were night landings. In the last 90 days; I had 5.6 hours in a C182 and 11 landings; 6 of which were night landings. Eight of the eleven landings in the prior 90 days; including all six of the night landings; took place one week before the occurrence; and those practice landings took place at ZZZ in nighttime crosswind conditions comparable to the date of the occurrence.I believe the occurrence was ultimately caused by pilot error; and better pilot actions at a couple different points in time could have potentially avoided the outcome. The initial opportunity could have been when I first experienced the gust (if it was a gust) and the resulting left yaw immediately before touchdown. Had my reaction been to add full power at that point; rather than attempt to correct the heading; the outcome might have been avoided. Likewise; had I not overcorrected with right aileron / under corrected with left rudder during the correction; I may have touched down aligned with the runway and avoided the sideloading upon touchdown. Additionally; had I immediately recognized the side loading force when it occurred and added the remaining available right aileron and left rudder without a couple seconds of delay; I may have timely offset the force and corrected the track of the rollout before the side loading became so strong that the right main gear left the runway pavement. In terms of future corrective actions; I plan to schedule some instructor time under crosswind conditions so the instructor can make a fresh evaluation of my crosswind landing technique to see if there are deficiencies I haven't recognized. As an additional step; I believe I'm going to obtain a tail wheel endorsement because I've heard and read that tailwheel training really enhances rudder skills during landing and taxi operations.

column121: Day 0; Learjet 60; departed ZZZ1 for ZZZ. The forecast for ZZZ indicated ¼ mile in FZFG which caused the crew to delay takeoff for 1 hour to allow our arrival at ZZZ for the estimated forecast at XA:00z to be 200 and ½ mile visibility. The crew departed ZZZ1 at XB:51z and arrived in the area at approximately XC:06z just after the control tower opened. The crew acknowledged the new ATIS '1' indicating winds Calm; ¼ FG; Ceiling 100; Temp -1C/Dewpoint -1C; and Altimeter 30.17. There was no mention of Freezing Fog. RNAV (GPS) Rwy XX was in use. The ILS Rwy XX Glidepath is NOTAM'd out of service. As a crew; we decided to 'take a look' and performed the approach. At minimums; the approach lights came into sight and then the runway was in sight. However; due to a loss of visual to the runway missed approach was conducted. During the missed approach the crew noticed the weather seemed to be improving. We talked about it and thought that we would be able to complete an approach and land. After being vectored to the final approach course by ZZZ Approach Control; we performed a second RNAV (GPS Rwy XX approach. On this approach; we again had the approach light system in sight at minimums and then the runway in sight. The Flying Pilot maintained a stabilized approach speed of approximately 140 Knots based on a calculated VREF speed of 137 Knots. During the landing flare the plane floated for about 2 to 3 seconds before touching down. The flying pilot immediately deployed the thrust reverser system and began braking. The Pilot Monitoring noticed the 1000 foot marker quickly approaching and made the callout. The Pilot Flying went to maximum braking and the aircraft overran the end of the runway approximately 20 feet in soft mud.The calculations from the aircrafts Aircraft Performance Program  indicated that based on the criteria of a wet runway and flaps 40° and using 115% performance numbers; our landing distance based on a 18;361 pounds was 3794 feet. Unfortunately; because of the 3 second of floating time; much of the runway was used up during the landing.After shutting down the engines and notifying the tower of the incident; we exited the runway to assess any damage and coordinate with our company to recover the aircraft. I noticed that the runway was very slick in spite of being grooved which I believed contributed to the overrun. No obvious damage was noticed and recovery efforts were accomplished with no further problems.

column121: Potential electrical hazard in the BK117C2/C2e. While checking aircraft battery voltage; I noticed the Caution and Advisory Display (CAD) had asymmetrical caution lights with the left side BUS TIE OPN caution not illuminated. After troubleshooting; I was able to determine the #1 Main Bus was hot when it should have been cold in this state. The cause was determined by Maintenance after extensive troubleshooting and effort to be a failure of the Bus Tie Control Relay in the Overhead Panel as it was generating power at all times causing the Bus Tie Relay to be closed at all times and rendering the BUS TIE switch inoperative. My concern is that our base pilots operating per the checklist for everyday operations close both bus ties and never noticed; nor should they have noticed; the anomaly with the aircraft. There are multiple electrical emergency procedures that would be affected by such an anomaly and I feel Airbus should consult as to whether or not they wish to change their guidance for preflight procedures as they did when they added the DC System Check" to the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the EC135 in the early 2000's. They should add a step in the normal procedures section of the RFM to pause when turning power on via the BAT MSTR switch in the "ON" position until the Central Panel Display System (CPDS) self-test is complete and ensure both BUS TIE OPN caution lights are illuminated before cycling the switch to the "Engage" position."

column121: After losing the left wheel on takeoff and successfully landing back at ZZZ airport the missing wheel was recovered. On inspection of the wheel it was noticed that the cotter pin for the wheel retaining collar was missing. I had removed the wheels recently to clean and check the brake linings and shoes to improve brake performance after a few flights and it appears that I did not replace the cotter pin on the left side. With the anti-clockwise rotation of the left wheel against the retaining collar it appears the collar became unscrewed causing the wheel to come off the axle.I do not know how I missed this when installing the wheel hub cap and dust plate.Lesson learned is to double check critical installations and even have a second person check the work.

column121: I arrived and began preflight planning for a maintenance flight to test a diode on the right engine. I conducted a weight and balance form; a dispatch sheet and spoke with maintenance about what had been done to the aircraft in order to plan accordingly. I planned to travel to the midway practice area and perform basic maneuvers to include steep turns; slow flight; and stalls at 3;000 feet over water southeast of ZZZ. I conducted a preflight and noted no defects with the airplane; all fluids were filled to an acceptable level and no notable damage was found. I got into the airplane and started the engines; taxied to the runup; completed the before takeoff check checklist and taxied to the runway without any issues. I did a normal takeoff from runway XX full length at ZZZ and noted no issues on the takeoff roll. Approach let me know that there were two other airplanes in the practice area so I talked to them and determined I would work the east side north south at 3;000 ft. I got into the practice area; got set up for maneuvers and started with steep turns. No issues with steep turns so I moved on to slow flight. Once I began slow flight I pulled the power to 25% load on each engine and lowered the landing gear handle. Upon landing gear extension I noticed a strange yaw to the left and looked down and noticed my right main landing gear position indicator light was not illuminated and my gear unsafe light was illuminated.I continued to fly south and I began to trouble shoot starting with the gear fire test button which illuminated all landing gear position indicator lights and proved that all lights were working. I then called Aircraft Y and asked if they could fly below me and check if my gear was down. They did and confirmed the right main was in the wheel well. I then asked if they noted any change as I ran the manual extension of landing gear checklist and pulled the manual extension handle. The pilot of Aircraft Y confirmed that the landing gear was still stuck in the up position. This confirmed that there was a real problem and I began to maneuver with the gear handle down in an effort to try to pull the landing gear out of the wheel well. Once I had tried this a few times I determined that it was not working and wanted an official answer from the tower confirming that the right main landing gear was stuck up. I swapped frequencies to approach control and requested priority handling requesting to return to ZZZ for a low pass. I did and the tower confirmed that the right main appeared to be in the wheel well.I responded to the tower that I would return to the midway practice area to troubleshoot and burn off fuel. I returned to the midway practice area; continued to maneuver the aircraft and asked over our company frequency if anyone could get maintenance on the radio. Maintenance had me try a few different methods to lower the gear including going 180 kts and lowering the landing gear; pushing the manual gear extension handle back in and cycling the gear a few different times and adding constant G forces in a 60 degree banked steep turn. None of these methods worked. Eventually Aircraft Z; containing a representative of the FSDO and my Chief Pilot; departed ZZZ and flew close to me while I troubleshot the problem. Once I had tried everything and burned 10 or more gallons of fuel; I determined that the gear was not going to come down. I then returned to ZZZ. I entered left traffic XX. On short final for XX ~100' I pulled the power to idle and turned off the left then right engine masters and landed. I opened the canopy as I was coming to a stop. Once stopped I turned off the electric master and departed the aircraft.

column121: My partner and I were assigned an ETOPS on Aircraft X. During our inspection; we found the crew O2 bottle was reading 1300 psi. We then replaced the bottle; no leaks noted; sitting in the cockpit and  completed the ETOPS check; and went to sign off paperwork. We received a gate call; from the flight crew; that the captains mask was leaking after he tested it. When we arrived to the cockpit; the captain had disconnected the mask; from the box; and explained to us that it wouldn't stop leaking. We then connected the mask; and saw that the mask was leaking; and disconnected it again; due to safety reasons; and not wanting to leave the mask connected and leaking. We went and ordered a mask; and replaced the mask; and no help. At that point we decided to change the stowage box; and at that point; I went downstairs; turned off the bottle; went back; replaced the box; and when I turned the bottle back on to leak check; all the other masks started leaking as well. When all 4 masks started leaking; the flight crew assisted me in disconnecting all the masks by the quick disconnects. The captain disconnected his; I disconnected the first and  second observers mask; and the other was disconnected by the relief pilot. I then contacted my Crew Chief; and when he came out; I wanted to show him what we had as a problem. When I reconnected the second observers mask; we had the flashover.

column121: After listening to the ATIS while in descent into VNY; I advised the PF that winds were from the north and visual approaches where being conducted to 34L. No approaches are available for that runway so I loaded a visual approach with a 5nm final. After gaining sight of the airport; ATC cleared us for the visual. We enter a base for a 5 mile final and began our descent. I check my iPad to find the altitude of the terrain we were over and determined the obstacles in the area were at about 2100' MSL; and we were currently a 3500' in a descent. column121: The engine startup; taxi; takeoff and climb out were all normal/standard. We headed south to the practice area and stayed a few miles south of Location X for the main body of the lesson. We performed Basic Attitude Instrument (BAI) maneuvers; GPS and VOR tracking and then climbed up to 6;500 feet. We performed 3 spins with climbs back to altitude in between with no engine changes. Afterwards we performed two unusual attitude recoveries. After the second recovery the engine RPM was unable to be recovered back to full power. It remained at 1;700 RPM at full throttle for the remainder of our flight back to ZZZ. As we noticed the problem; I took control from my student and turned direct to ZZZ. We began trouble shooting by activating the fuel prime; exercising the throttle and changing to the alternate air source. We pitched for best glide airspeed and continued to the airport. We were unable to maintain altitude and remained in a constant descent at around 100 feet per minute. The wind was very light so we took the left base for runway XXL when offered by the tower; as it was closer than entering for XYR. We held our altitude from 3;500 to 3;000 as we continued to the left base. Upon reaching the left base we descended and entered a slip to make the runway while keeping as much altitude as possible. On the base to final turn with the power reduced we heard a slight knocking noise coming from the engine. We asked the tower if they could make out any loose parts on our nose but they reported nothing. The landing was standard with no issue. Upon landing the rpm fell well below the normal 1;000 RPM idle to only 600 RPM. We saw no other issues so we taxied to the ramp and shut down. After landing we saw oil coating the starboard side of our belly and the landing strut.

column121: On Day 2; I was assigned to build Pratt & Whitney 4060 HPT (Hight Pressure Turbine) module. There were three cardboard boxes stacked on a wooden pallet. The lowest box contained the T2 rotating airseal; the middle box contained the T1 outer airseal; and the top box contained the T2 retaining plate. The boxes were not secured to the pallet; which has not been an issue in the past.Previously; on Day 0; I had opened the top box containing the T2 retaining plate (P/N XXXXXX); installed the plate and placed the empty box back on top of the other two. On Day 2; I opened the box containing the T1 outer airseal; visually inspected the part and noticed an area on the edge that was dented and had raised metal. Looking closer I noticed it was cracked. Inspection looked at the damage; rejected the part and placed the item on pending Engineering review. On Day 3; I removed the bottom box containing the T2 rotating airseal and immediately noticed a grey powder near the edge of the part. The edge had what appeared to be a dent approx. 2' long and a rough; jagged area about the same length as the dent. Inspection looked at the damage; rejected the part and placed the part on pending Engineering review. It appears that both parts suffered impact damage with a hard surface; probably concrete. All three items were made serviceable on different dates; so it is unlikely that they were damaged before or during their short stay in the stockroom. The logical conclusion is that the parts were pulled from stock; placed on the pallet and then fell off the pallet during transport from the stockroom to the build area. The cardboard box for the T2 rotating airseal had grey powder along the cut in the box; indicating the part came through the box; impacted; and then was pushed back into the box.Although having damaged parts is never a good thing; I am more concerned with the fact that someone knew these parts had fallen off the pallet and then placed them back inside the box and there was no follow-up to ensure the items were still serviceable. Was this accident brought to Management's attention or did the employee; fearing loss of his job; try and hide what happened? Once Inspection looked at the parts; it was immediately clear the parts were not serviceable; so I highly doubt anyone bothered to get Inspection involved. Furthermore; these parts still had serviceable tags on them; meaning the Inspectors who made them serviceable were placed in jeopardy by someone else's deliberate carelessness. Lastly; if I had not seen the damage and installed the parts; then my job would have been in jeopardy also. If I sound upset; it's because I am: hiding damaged parts is crossing the line and doing so endangers other employee's careers and puts our passenger's safety at risk.Suggested Resolution: The Company needs to do a better job communicating that damaged parts must be brought to the attention of Management; and Management must get Inspection or Engineering involved before proceeding. Early in my career it was drilled into me that you won't get fired for damaging a part; but you will get fired if you try and hide it. It appears the company is not doing a good enough job of ensuring this is well known amongst all employees.

Once we confirmed the traffic had passed and there was no longer a conflict; we climbed back to assigned altitude.No further instructions or concerns were communicated by Approach at that time. column121: I was a student solo. I had informed tower before my initial takeoff with callsign 'Student Solo Aircraft X holding short; RWY 17.' After receiving clearance for takeoff and my readback; I said; 'wish me luck.' On my third landing to complete my solo; I was on short final about 150ft above the ground and about 0.25 miles from the runway threshold for RWY 17. When the controller told me to 'make a left three-sixty.' He informed me that he wanted me to make space for inbound traffic behind me that was a faster plane and was not in the closed traffic. As he described to me; in his thinking; inbound traffic should have priority over pattern work. I reminded him that the lowest aircraft has right of way; and I was on short final for landing. As I turned; I attempted to arrest my descent; increase airspeed; reconfigure the aircraft (flaps; carb heat); turn; and climb all at a very low altitude and slow airspeed (approximately 60kts). The maneuver caused a loss of airspeed (as low as 50kts); nearly stalling the plane. I leveled the wings (at approximately 360 heading) to regain vertical lift and lowered the nose to allow the airspeed to increase. Once I felt the plane was safe; I continued my 360-turn to the left. As I resumed my left turn and reached approximately a 280 heading; I observed Aircraft Y approaching from my right; and it was evident that continuing my turn would result in a mid-air collision. I took evasive action by turning to the right. Within a few seconds of my evasive maneuver the controller asked me to 'turn a little to the northeast' which would be a right turn from my current heading. As indicated above; I had already initiated that turn to the right/NE. After this near miss; I was instructed to resume landing following a helicopter. I knew the rotor would create heavy turbulence; so I extended my downwind significantly to allow time for the turbulence to dissipate. However; I still experienced significant turbulence on final approach and chose to go-around. I believe that this controller made several mistakes that endangered me as a student. I believe it would have been unacceptable even for an experienced pilot to be turned away on short final like that.

column121: We operated Aircraft X to DEN in VMC conditions.  All required checklists and briefings were completed.  We conducted the SSKII 4 RNAV arrival into DEN and was subsequently being vectored for the RNAV Y Runway 16R approach.While being vectored; ATC issued a descent instruction. We believed the clearance was to descend to 5;000 feet MSL.  The assigned altitude was read back as 5;000 feet MSL; and no correction was provided by ATC.  We believed the altitude assignment had been correctly received and acknowledged.  We did not question the clearance at the time because it was acknowledged when received.  Additionally; based on the altitude to lose and the phase of flight; 5;000 feet MSL appeared reasonable at that moment.The flight remained in VMC conditions.  It was at that point while descending through approximately 6;500 feet MSL; we began discussing that the assigned altitude and how it seemed lower than expected given the aircraft's distance from the DEN airport (which was in sight during the descent).  Before we could query ATC regarding the altitude assignment; ATC made contact; stated they received a low altitude alert; and instructed the us to level off at 6;000 feet MSL and asked whether the airport was in sight. The flight was thereafter cleared for a visual approach to Runway 16R and landed without further incident.This event served as a learning experience. Although thorough arrival and approach briefings had been conducted; in the future I will place additional emphasis on reviewing and cross-checking instrument approach procedure altitudes; even when operating in VMC.  This includes recognizing the significance of published altitudes; as well as maintaining heightened awareness of airport elevation and surrounding terrain. As a Captain; I will continue to promote effective crew resource management by encouraging open communication on the flight deck and maintaining a strong focus on situational awareness and operational safety.
